All tender and generous emotions are first discoverable in the behaviour, afterwards in action. Respect, esteem, love, compassion cannot wait for an opportunity of doing something for their object; they beam on the countenance; they express themselves in motions and attitudes and tones of voice ; they give birth to countless trifling tokens of their presence; they shine forth in the cordial grasp of the hand, in the warm embrace, in the responsive smile or tear, in the glad offer of the warmest corner or the softest seat, or the most desirable position. All those myriad little acts which we include under the name of politeness or courtesy are the natural fruits of a loving and benevolent spirit, ar d a delicate appreciation. ELOQUENCE.—" Eloquent!" said the Chicago lawyer of , his partner. "He's able to reason the kick out of a mule. Why, here a while ago business was dull, and he decided that Mrs. Dasher ought to have a divorce, and he'd go into court and get it for her, and then charge her for it. Some- how she heard what was going on. She galloped down to the court-house to stop him, as she didn't want a divorce. She got there just as he was making his plea for her. And mind you, she was mad at him, but by Jove, sir, she listened to him five minutes and became so convinced that she ought to have a divorce that she walked right up where the jury could see her and shed three pints of tears while he recited her wrongs. And when he won the case she embraced him, and said he should conduct all her divorce cases. I call that eloquence." As an example of the influence of the Jews among the ignorant Russian peasantry, the following characteristic story is worth columns of explanation :—A peasant goes to a Jew in an adjoining village Ind asks for the loan of a rouble to buy vodka. The Jew consents to lend the rouble, but requires sectrity, and olers to take the peasant's sheepskin coat in pawn. The neasant returns for his coat and gives it to the Jew in exchange for a rouble. The latter, however, lends the rouble on the security of the sheepskin only at the usual 100 per cent. interest, and tells the peasant that when he comes to claim his coat he must pay back the rouble I,,nt and another rouble besides for the loan. The peasant understands, and goes away with the rouble. Belo ehe gets far away the Jew calls him back and says, "V. at an idiot you are! Give me back now the rouble which I have just given you, as you will only spend it all in drink, and you will then have only one rouble to pay me when you come for your coat." The peasant, completely taken is by this logic, gives back the rouble and goes home to his friends. When he has told them what he has done, some one exclaims, " Bow is it that you bring nothing back? You bring no money, no vodka, you still owe the Jew a rouble, and you have lost your coat." The dull pea- nut scratches his head and replies," I really don't know myself how it has been done, but the Jew was perfectly right in his calculation. FERNS PROPAGATED BY Currnios.—lt is generally known that ferns may be propagated from cuttings of the fronds? At the instance of an acquaintance we made the experiment with about three inches of a bipinnate frond. The pinnse of one side were cut off, the rib laid lengthwise, with its extremities a little deeper in the soil, and an inverted tumb- ler put over it to keep it moist. In a short time small fronds were developed from the base of the remaining pinnw. A Youso Cucaroo.—Last autumn, a young cuckoo was taken at Westbourne and carefully cherished during the past severe winter. it was allowed to fly about in an open hall, and has become so tame that it will perch on the finger and permit itself to be stroked. It will also occasionally sit on a cat's back. It is fond of boiled egg, and delights in the caterpillars of the "woolly bear." Jenyns observes that the orbits of the mature bird are orange-yellow; these are of a pale citron. The irides, as he describes them' are at present liver brown. Its cuckoo cry has not yet been heard. LANCASHIRE AGRICULTURE.—Fine weather is much wanted for hay making. There is a great deal of grass down between the Mersey and the Ribble. The grass is generally very thin, and much below the average, the ground being quite green after the scythe. On the north side of the Ribble there is a good average crop of hay grass, and in a number of places the meadows are very heavy, and the grass laid. Hay-making is not quite BO far advanced as on the south side ef the river, but many farmers were pre- pared to commence early this week if the weather was at all favourable. There is much difference in the readiness of grass for the scythe, but it is gsnerally later than the aver- age, and complaints are made of the grass being tough. In some meadows the seed grass is quite brown ripe, while there is very little bottom grass. The excessive number of butter- cups in the hay grass this year will not improve the quality. On the north side of the Ribble grain is much later—in some cases as much as a month—than on the Ormsk irk side. But very little grain is grown there. The Fylde, which used to be called "the granary of Lancashire," has gone rapidly of late to dairying, and it is only in places where the land is specially favourable to the plough that wheat is grown. There is a great tendency to make cheese in pre- ference to selling milk and butter, the former being con- sidered the more profitable. Potatoes are not looking so well in the Fylde as in most other places, and there have been a few unsound ones found. In some places there will be a fair quantity of pears and stone fruit, but other kinds of fruit will be scarcer. A great many apples have dropped from the trees in the Fylde orchards within the last ten days or a fortnight. Farmers are speaking a little more hopefully of their prospects than they have done for the last two or three years, but much yet depends upon the weather. Caoss BREEDING evils SHEEP.—The most successful example of cross breeding with a view to the establishment of a distinct breed is undoubtedly that of the Oxford Down, and probably the late Mr. S. Diane, of Eynsham, was one of its earliest promoters ; but as he himself states, several of his neighbours at the same time adopted the cross—that is, the Hampshire Down ewe and the Cotswold ram improved by the Leicester. Somewhat previous to this Mr. W. T. Twynam, in North Hampshire, commenced the cross, and followed it for some six years, durffig which time he sold rams to more than eighty flockmasters, most of them owners of Hampshire Down flocks; so that, although be might in- directly have contributed to the Oxford breed, he principally diffused his breed amongst the Hampshire and Wiltshire flocks, which no doubt tended to the enlargement of the size, the growth of the wool, and the improvement of the carcase. 3 have in my possession a list of some eighty floekmasters who purchased his rams. It would appear that the days of bargaining are not yet over, for the other day an elderly spinster entered a sta- tioner's shop in Kensington, and asked to look at some note- paper. " How much a quire ?" said she. "Sixpence," said the assistant. " I'll give you fourpence," quoth the elderly one. " I beg your pardon," said the assistant, " I made a mistake—the price is threepence per quire." "0, then, I'll give you twopence," as promptly replied the un- abashed spinster. She was evidently one of the old school.

NEW (?) USE FOR ALAUNACES.—A stationer in an Essex country town, who for many years had issued a hanging wall almanack printed upon goed old-fashioned cardboard, which had always been received with great favour, last year tried a better design, ad attempted to cover the extra cost , by the use of thinner board. Be found, however, that it would not do, and complaints were loud indeed, some of the farmers going so far as to send the " rubbishing things" back. The stationer tried to explain that the almanack was better, but his excuse was received with supercilious con- tempt, till light was at last let in as to the reason of the grumbling by one of the burly malcontents declaring that "if three of them almanacks was pasted together they might be thick enough, but for his part he pref4red the old sort," and then it dawned upon the poor stationer 'that the keen appreciation shown for his good old-fashioned almanacks on good old-fashioned cardboard meant—gun- wads I • SUNSHINE OF 1881.—The Right Hon. the Speaker has published the following figures, in which the hours of sun- shine of the first six months of the current year are com- pared with those of the two preceding years. The Greenwich and the Glynde instruments are the only ones of which any public record exists, and the experience at Glynde probably more nearly represents the truth for the south-east of Eng- land than that of Greetwich, where river fogs may be sup- posed to diminish the hours of sunshine below the average truth of the country. It will be seen that the amount of Isunshine for the first half of this year exceeds by nearly 50 per cent, that of 1879 for the same period.

1879. 1880. 1881. January February March April May June Total A PRINTER'S JOKE.—Printer's jokes are not always en- joyable, but an exception may be made in favour of the witticisms of John B. Tolman, of Lynn, U.S., who celebrated his golden wedding by giving 2,500d015. to the city hos- pital, to be used for the benefit of the printers of Lynn, ac- companying the gift with the following note:—" Gentle- men,—Having been a pioneer in the printing business in Lynn and having spent a long term of years in the (to me) pleasant application of the "Art Preservative of all Arts," and as my wife belongs to a typographical family repro- eented by a father and four (of six) brothers, I have im- proved the " golden " epportunity—vouchsafed but once in a lifetime—to commemmorate the 50th anniversary of our marriage by a gift to the Lynn Hospital in behalf of the 1 printers of Lynn. I. therefore, have this day "given out" to the Lynn Hospital a "take" of 2,500d015. to be "set up" and remain as "live matter," to be" worked off" as occa- sion may require, but in no "case is the original " forme " to be "distributed." I cherish the hope, for your sake, that the institution may never be obliged to " turn " for want of "sorts," or have the misfortune to "pie the forme" , or " squabble" any part; but will beep the" furniture " so well "adjusted," and so ply the " mallet " and " shooting- ' stick " that not a " quoin " shall "drop out" or be lost. Thus may they be able to "work off" " token " after "token" year by year, till the last living member of the "black art" shall have " corrected " his last "proof."

STATE OF Bustnise.—The PRIME MINISTER intimated that as soon as Committee on the Land Bill had elostd the Government would. take Supply. Mondav would be devoted to the Transvaal debate. Should that conclude on the satne night the report of the Land Bill would be taken on Tuesday and, Wednesday, and he hoped they would be able to takilf the third reading on the following day. THE lam LAND, BILL.—The House again went into Committeeun the Land Bill, and resumed the consieeration of the new daises. Iti the course of the evening Mr. HEALY asked whether the Government would, adhere to the first part of their bill in substance in the event of itsbeing thrown out by the Lords.—Mr. GLaustomt replied that the Gov- ernment would do all in their power to procure the accept- ance of their measure, and hoped it would not miscarry; but he declined to forecast what would occur ia a conting- ency which he trusted they would not anticipate. 'THE MODEL LOCOMOTIVE ENGINEER, FIREMAN, AND ENGINE' BOY (London: Crliby4Aawood, and Co).—This interesting work contains an'historical notice of the pioneer lolcomotive engines and their inventors, which is really well Written. The volume also contains a project for the esta- liishment of certificates of qualification in the running ger- vice-of .railways well worthy of the careful and thoughtful perusal of those concerned. It is the work of Mr. Michael: Reynolds, formerly locomotive inspector on the London, Brighton, and South Coast Railway, and we congratulate him on having produced an eminently practical volume writtea in an attractive style which cannot fail to recom- rnentlit to all who are engaged in the profession of an engine driver. The subject is a novel one, which should interest a large portion of the general public, seeing that the men whom it immediately concerns have the lives of thousands of peOpla in, their bands to a very great' extent, and we cannot belp,thinking that if the rules andcautions laid down by the author were incorporated b the every day working of our engine drivers, the dangeraattendant upon railway travelling would be materially lessened and the number of accidents greatly reduced. , ExEtrEtrrs or GEOGRAPHY (London: Crosby, Lockwood, Co.).—This is a cheap and useful little book by the Rev. B. J. Johns, simply and systematically arranged and suitable •iaa text book for elementary teachers. The author has evidently bestowed much care in collecting his information on population and political facts.._ _

V-mtrtottost NEW TasriaiENT (London: Eyre and Spot- t iswoode).—The issue of the Variorum New Testament in a separate form, which has hitherto been issued only as pert vf the Variorum Teacher's Bible, cannot fail to be regarded hy the religious world sea happy thefight on the part of the enterprising publishers. It will be a valuable aid to enable Bilde students to judge of the value of the New Revision of the New Testament, which has recently been published, who can test the practical value of this edition by taking a diffi- cult chapter and seeing how the obscurities are almost always cleared away one after another. Those who do this will agree with QS in saying that it is an invaluable com- panion to the thoughtful intelligent reader of the sacred volume. In this edition are collated 15 ancient and 54 modern commentators, 6 versions, 33 ancient manuscripts, and 9 critical editions of the text. It is edited by three eminent scholars who have evidently done their work well and carefully. This work consists of the Authorised Version with marginal references, and a complete selection in Eng- lish of V 4710118 readings and renderings from the hest authorities, by way of footnotes. Variations of rendering Ire given Where the Authorised Version is not held to re- present the original fairly; variations of reading where there seems reason to correct the original used by the translators of the Authorised Version. The Variorum footnotes sum- marise for the reader unacquainted with the Hebrew or Greek languages the surest results of Hebrew and Greek scholarship and of the study of ancient MSS. and versione, knd point out the degree of authority. attaching to each rendering or reading. The alternative translations will often render note or comment needless, and suggest, possibly tor the first time, the full meaning of a passage.
ST. HELENS FREE LIERAIiY.
PROPOSED IMPORTANT CHANGES.

The monthly meeting of the Library Committee was held on Wednesday, Mr. H. R. Ltcey presiding. There were also present Councillors Brook, and Fisher; Messrs..Drom- goole, N. Lacey, and Sinclair. Mr. Oulu (deputy town clerk) read the following report of the sub-committee :—Report of the sub-committee ap- pointed to prepare a catalogue for the St. Helens Free Public Library. The sub-committee have met from time to time since their appointment and have given consideration to the matter& referred to them. They have appointed James McNabb, of St. Helens, to compile the catalogue under their direction and superintendence at the salary of ss. per day. The sub-committee have inspected the libraries in several ' adjoining towns.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: STATE OF IRELAND.

What was reported on Saturday as a terrible double murder at Doon, county Limerick, is now said to have been a purely accidental occurrence. A young man named , Richardson was driving his uncle to Bilboa, near noon, on Wednesday, when the car was accidentally overturned, and the two Richardson's received such serious injuries that the younger one died on Friday and the other on Monday. On Saturday an inquiry was opened, and after hearing medical evidence an adjournment for a week was agreed to. On SaturdaY Mr. Dalttest'one of the" suspects" lodged in Kil- mainham prison, Was released owing to ill-health. A shocking murder was committed near &Rebore, County Cavan, on Monday night. A man named Lynch was on his way home from market, when be was fired at, and shot dead. The murder is attributed in the district to Ribbonism. Five arrests have been made. At Mayo Assizes, on Tuesday, P. J. Gordon, one of the Land League traversers, was charged with inciting others to kill Walter M. Bourke, a landlord, living near Claremorris. 'He was further charged with inciting others to murder Mr. Herbert Davis, of Ballybanuis. On this count prisoner was found guilty. Sentence was deferred. The case excited the utmost interest, the court being crowded to excess. At Cork Assizes, on Tuesday, in the case against O'Gor- man, the hotel proprietor, Charleville, for refusing to enter- tain Property Defence representatives on the eve of an execution sale, the jury disagreed. Judge Barry described the result as very appalling. The only question left to the jury to decide was whether O'Gorman, refused accommoda- tion to these gentlemen. The whole of the evidence proved he did, and prisoner's counsel conceded it. He deplored the result deeply, for the sake of the country and for the sake of trial by jury, which he valued more than any of them, and which was the.great support ef their liberty. TIM TRIM Pizzas ON THE LAND Comutssimanns.—The Irish Times, commenting on the Irish Land Commission, says it is not a strong one, and believes the large social re- construction which the Land Act promises will lack the authority which would have attached to it ,if ,tbe,Cominis- sion bad been of greater weight. It considers that a judge of the Supreme Cnurt of Judicature ought to have been appointed. The Freeman, while agreeing that the Commis- sion is a weak one, thinks it only fan' to say the gentlemen composing it can stand the test of criticism. At the Castlebar Assizes Patrick J. Gordon, one of the persons arrested under the Protection Act, was indicted for inciting to murder. The curcumstances were somewhat peculiar. Gordon was arrested on the 13th of April under Lord Cowper's warrant, and on the way from Clarmorris to Galway he addressed the crowd at several stations, advising them to shoot their landlords; and at Ballyhannis he re- ferred particular to Mr, Liable Davies, saying he hoped to hear that gentleman had been shot. The Jury found the accused guilty, and he was sentenced to a year's imprison- ment with hard labour. On Sanday night, at Corbally, a suburb of Limerick, Patrick Ryan, land bailiff, who has acted at most of the evictions that have recently taken place in the county of Limerick, was waylaid.by a number of men, who attacked him with loaded sticks and beat him most unmercifully. He was knocked down, and kicked white on the ground. 'Ryan is in such a dangerous condition that his depositions were taken on Monday before a magistrate. Patrick Shannon, a farmer's son, has been irrested for complicity in the out- rage, and the police are in search of others. Mr. Justice Barry, addressing the grand jury at Cork assizes on Monday, said that out of 50 indictments 35, though technically of a minor character, indicated a most disorgan- ised state of society, and though they were not of an agra- rian character, they arose from persons taking advantage of Ihe present agitatir n to carry on private purposes The cases reported by the constabulary were in the West Riding 120, as against 30 last year, and in the East Riding 134, agtinst 67. He would still express a hone that the worst had pissed but the prospect was anything but cheering.
THREATENING TO MURDER Tin CHIEF SECRETARY FOR IRELAND.

A youth named Hickie, describing himself as of no home or occupation, was charged at the Bow-street Police Court, London, on Tuesday, with threatening to murder Mr. For- ster. The Chief Secretary received a letter from "P.T.H.," inviting him toe duel, and informing him that unless he ac- cepted this challenge or released the prisoners arrested under the Coercion Act, he would have to "die like a dog." The prisoner had previously applied to the Commissioners of Police for an appointment, and it was alleged that the hand- writing of the applicamt on that occasion corresponded with the handwriting of the threatening letter. The police received another communication, signed by "An Honest Englishman," who professed to have overheard a conversation between the prisoner and a man in a public-house at Brixton with reference to the shoot- ing of " tbat tyrant Buckshot Forster." "An Honest Englishman" enclosed a letter which he stated he had "picked up," and which was addressed by "Ps 'rick P. Hickie" to "Dear Malachi." In this letter the writer urged that Forster "must be killed at any rate; and added, "I will be prepared for him on Sunday next: I will watch him when coming from his prayers." The prisoner was is. mended; and until further evidence is adduced that the 'Honest Englishman" who anonymously communicated to the police the threatening letter he professes to have "picked up" is forthconing, it will be difficult to form any estimate as to the gravity of the case.

SOUTHPORT.

On the 30th May, 1861.-,ll3.Q;Committee visited South- port and were received by Alderman Nicholson, the chair- man of the Library Committee, and shown over the various departments of the Southport Free Library. The library contains 10,132 volumes, of which 2,263 are donations con- tributed by ladies and gentlemen of the town and neighbour- hood. In the issue of books from the lending department the committee have dispensed with the indicator for want of space, and borrowers names, and addresses, and occupations are entered in a book. Thee is a good reference library, and the committee are now fitting up a room for the con- venience of those who may desire to use this department for the purpose of study or otherwise. In connection with the library are also two reading rooms—one for magazines and periodicals, and the other for newspapars exclusively. There is a branch library at Churclatown which is proving very use- ful in that locality.

div.head: BOLTON.
div.p: BOLTON.

The sub-committee also visited on the same day the Bolton Free Public Library where they were met by the chairman of the Library Committee of the borough, Mr. Alderman Greenhalgh, and the librarian. The sub-committee were conducted through the reference library and reading rooms in the Town Hall square, and subsequently through the lending library in another part of the town, and in premises formerly occupied by the Mechanics' Institute. They also visited the branch library at Little Bolton. All information sought respecting the arrangement and management of the library, was very willingly accorded by Mr. Greenhalgh and the librarian. The books at each of the libraries are placed on shelves around the various rooms. The shelves are ar- ranged on what is known as the "press "system; that is the shelves are divided into sections of pretty equal width from the floor to the ceiling. Each of these sectiens is called a press and is known by a number. The shelves on the several presses are distinguished by letters and the books on each shelf are numbered consecutively, the numbering en each shelf commencing at "1," so that if a reader requires a book on applying for it he quotes, say "16k 9, which means thatthe book he requires is to be found in Dress 16 shelf D, and that the number of the book is 9. The chief advantage in this system appeared to be in the fact that by the use of it shelf space could be economised with areater advantage by arranging the books according to size and subject. The catalogues are arranged alphabetically without regard to classification (1) under author's name; (2) under the title of the book ; and in some cases (3) under the subject. There is a record kept by the librarian of the class of literature issued under the following heads:— Theology, philosophy, English history, foreign history, biography, topography, voyages and travels, law, politics, and commerce, science and the arts, poetry and the drama, novels and romances, magazines, and general literature. There are in the reference library and reading room 27,526 volumes, exclusive of those in a department known as the subscription library. There is in connection with the re- ference library a reading-room, students'-room, and subscrip- tion librstry. The latter is exclusively for subscribers, and is managed by a committee of which one-third are mem- bers of the Library Committee and two-thirds are elected by the subscribers. It is under the care of the librarian of the Free Library. Thete are at the present time 370 subscribers at £1 Is. per annum each. This represents the purchase of over £370 worth of books per annum, which at the end of each year are handed over to the corporation for the Public Library in return for the services of the librarian, use of room, tee. The subscribers have a threefold advantage. They are entitled to have for home reading first a work from the subscription library ; second, (with certain excep- tions) a volume from the reference library ; and third, one of the current magazines. The lending library is conducted as to the issue of the books much in the same manner as other lending libraries. The indicator system is used here. The indicator is something like the one in use at the St. Helens Library, except-that the soaces are arranged verti- cally instead of horizontally, and is a model af the shelves or presses. The branch library at Little Belton has been established several years in premises formerly used as the Little Bolton Town Hall, and consists of lending library and spacious reading-rooms formerly used as court-rooms. The arrangements here are in keeping with those at the chief libraries. The sub-committee noticed a number of youths (librarian's assistants) at the reference library and reading- room in the Town Hall square engaged in binding and re- pairing books, and the librarian stated that all ordinary binding and repairs of books in the library were executed by the youths in the spare hours of the day, Your committee suggests that this point should not be lost sight of for future use. Another feature in the excellent and careful management of the Bolton libraries is the covering of the works with cotton or linen cloth of a light colour, which not only strengthens the cheap binding, in which many new books are used, but gives a cleanly appearance to the library, while it also pre- serves the better bindings of tha more expensive works. The number and reference letter are stencilled on the backs instead of being written or print, d on bits of ground paper, and when the covers are dirty they are easily replaced., These libraries contain near upon 50,000 volumes to every 1.000 of the population. The average daily issues for the year 1881 were 530, and the number of volumes added was 887 by purchase and donation, and 724 by transfer from the subscription lihraty, making a total of 1,611 volumes. The ample provision thus supplied for the moral and intellec- tual requirements of the town reflects the highest credit on the Town Council and Library Committee, and an institu- tion so complete in all ite details cannot fail to leave its mark for good, permanently, on the character of the com- munity.

div.head: LIVERPOOL.
div.p: LIVERPOOL.

• On the 7th day of June the sub-committee visited the reading room of the Free Public Library in William Brown- street, Liverpool, and the Picton Reading-room adjoining. Mr. Connell, the chief librarian, received the sub-committee, and explained the workings of the institution. The books are divided into 16 classes, distinguished by letters—A to P —and are arranged according to such classes in department on the shelves, each class being numbered consecutively, from 1 upwards. The catalogue is an alphabetteal one, and has been compiled regardless of classes. Each book is con- tained in the catalogue,—lst under its author's name, 2nd under ita title, and 3rd under the subject thereof; and in some instances there is a 4 and 5 reference to particular works. The periodicals, instead of being left on the tables in the reading room for reference, as in the St. Helens Free Library reading room, are placed in wooden covers or other strong covers, and are under the charge of a boy, who issues them in the same manner as the books, and a record is kept of the issues. With the ilea of preventing any book or periodical being taken dway from the library the following system is adopted. Each person on entering the reading room has a- metallic cheek about the size of a penny given to him. On obtaining a book the check is aiven by the borrower to the assistant, by whom the book is issued. When the book is returned the check is given back to the borrower, who, on quitting the reading room, leaves it with the door keeper; thus every person leaving the read- ing room is required to produce on leaving either a check or a book. In the Plcton reading room a printed form on a slip of paper, which is filled in by the borrower with the number of the book borrowed, takes the place of the check, and is delivered up with the book. The sub-committee sub- sequently accompanied Mr. Cowell to the North End Branch .Lending Library in Great Nelson-street. This was purely a lending library, containing upwards of 21,657 vols. The 1 catalogue here is arranged in classes, each Class being num- bered separately from I. upwards; each book appears in the catalogue under its title and author. The indicator system Is not used at this library, but each issue is entered with the borrower's name and the number of the book on the list. Mr . Cowell, however, recommended to the sub-committee if they preferred the indicator system an indicator recently improved or invented, and used by the librarian of the Rich- mond (Surrey) Free Library. Both in Liverpool and Bolton the reference libraries contain complete sets of the Blue Book edition of patents, but in both places your sub- committee were advised not to cumber your shelves with them.

div.head: MANCHESTER.
div.p: MANCHESTER.

On the 14th day of June the sub-committee visited Man- chester,and attended, by appointment, at the Town Hall, where they were received by Mr. Alderman Baker, Mayor of Manchester, by whom the sub-committee were introduced to the chief librarian of the Manchester free libraries (Mr. fiuttcill). The sub-committee visited, with Mr. Sutton, the reference library in the old Town Hall building, and subse- quently the Hnlme Branch Library at the Hulme Town Hall. This latter is both a reference and a lending library. It contains 16,000 volumes. There is no indicator, in use here, each issue being entered on a list similar to that in the North Lending Library, Liverpool, but containing borrowers' name and number, and number of book, and its number 'which entails a coasiderable amount of bookkeeping. The e italogue is arranged in one alphabetical lot, and although he books are divided into classes, this is not regarded in the arrangement of the catalogue. Each class and author is nrranged as far as practicable by itself on the shelves, and numbered separately. In the else of popular literature, '? he hooks are also shelved under the authors name so that. (tor instance, if a borrower wishes to know if any of Mrs. ii-lenry Wood's works are in the Library the librarian by booking at the shelves allotted to her works can reply 'yes>, ,r," no" directly. There is in connection with this branch 'Library a youths' reading-room, which is set apart eaelu- ,iyely for boys and youths who are prohibited from using be general reading-room. The sub-committee noticed that ',ere, as in ,Liyerpool, the periodicals in the reading-room vere in wooden covers. On the same day the sub-Committee v;eited the Free Library and Reading-Room in Peel Park, `alford. and found the system of management similar to that . . .

the Halms Brancli-Lrary, except that the catalogue -o-f e Lending Library jdivided into daises, and issued into 40 prta—partJ being , catalogue of class J. (works of iction), and part 11. of the remaining 'glasses of the Library. *he librarian asked the sub-committee to accept from halt as a present to the St. Helens Free Public Library a copy of

"Memorial Statues of the Royal Free Museum and Library, Peel Park, Salford." The sub•committee accepted the &nip., and have now much pleasure in submitting it. The chief librarian and curator, Mr. Plant, considered " Woking " better rhtahratnh et hie° !en de ifcaat o br eseyks twe tans, aanad ebox et ehe dhe and ing M said ly rare r Sutton . occur- rence with them. On the subject of the "patents," he con- sidered them a very valuable acquisition to their Library, and stated that they were frequently consulted. In conclusion, the deputation, while expressing their gratifi- cation at the efforts made in the various towns visited to convey the treasures of learning and the irluence of litem- ture to the great mass of the people,feel that the resources of our St. Helens Free Library are far too limited, providing for about 10 per cent of the population, while Bolton pro- vides for 50 per cent. Class B: Science and Art, Commerce, Statistics, Natural History. Class C: Theology, Novels, Metaphysics, Political Economy. Class D: Fiction, Poetry, Drama. 3rd. PAVING, 87. c., COMMITTEE.
The monthly meeting of this committee was held on Wed- nesday, Alderman Johnson presiding. There were also present Alderman Cook, Councillors Bels her, Wilcock, and Foster.

div.head: CLAIM OF LANDS.
div.p: CLAIM OF LANDS.

Mr. CRAM said that at the last meeting it was stated that Messrs. Evans and Co. had deposited waste lime on a piece of land at Parr, of which the Corporation considered they were the owners; and it was resolved that Messrs. Evans be ordered to remove the lime. A letter having been sent to this effect, Messrs. Evans now replied declining to do as the Corpotation requested, as they and their predecessors had used the land for the last 50 years. Under these circum- stances they considered they were more entitled to the land than the Corporation, and they could only add that if the Corporation took legal proceedings they would defend the ease.—A short conversation took place, which the reporters were requested not to publish, and ultimately the Town Clerk and the Surveyor were directed to obtain all necessary information reguired in the event of legal proceedings being commenced.

AN ACCIDENT IN BOUNDARY ROAD. A letter was read from Mr. Riley, solicitor, stating that while Mrs. Lyon. Queen's Park, wasdriving along Boundary- road, the horse fell on account of the road giving way, and serious injuries were sustained by the horse and the coach- min. who fell off his seat over the horse. A sewer having been recently laid the horse's legs sank several inches and caused the accident —Mr. BREWIS wrote Mr. Riley saying that the road was at presont in the charge of Mr. Cowburn, contractor, and repudiated all liability on the part of the Corporation.—The action of the Town Clerk wasapproved.

The SURVEYOR said this month he had no cases of over- crowded yards to report, with the exception of one in Baxter's-lant), Sutton. Of course, there were small temporary erections, which were, however, unworthy of notice. This one in Baxter's-lane was of importance, consequent npon pigs being kept inside, and there being no proper means of drainage, the smell was very disagreeable. A notice was ordered to be served, directing the removal oi the piggery.

div.head: SECOND ST. HELENS L. E. V.
div.p: SECOND ST. HELENS L. E. V.

On Saturday afternoon the annual inspecti6n of the second Lancashire Engineer Volunteers was made by Colonel Hard- ing Steward, R.E., of Manchester, in a field at St. Ann's, belonging to Mr. Fishwick. At half-past three the members assembled at the Engineer Hall, and were after- wards put through some exercises in the drill ground adjoining. On the ground two bridges were constructed,—a barrel pier bridge, with two rafts, and two stays, for crossing water; a double lock bridge 50 feet span a single sling bridge 50 feet span, an American tension bridge, 50 feet ;long, and a trestle bridge, 33 feet long. The order of the companies to march over the bridges had been given, and the first company got upon the double lock bridge when one of the spans snapped nearly in two. About' one half of the company continued to march while the other half retreated akthe command of the officer. The piece of wood was afterwards examined by the inspector, and it was explained that the timber was very old, having been in constant use for the last ten years at the drill hall. The in- spector in the course of the afternoon elLarnined models which had been constructed by some of the members, and prizes were awarded as follows :—let prize, double lock bridge 40 feet span, Sergeant Burdekin ; 2nd, suspension bridge 200 feet span, by the same member; 3rd, suspension bridge, 100 feet span, Sapper Bennett. A march was then made by way of Eccleston-street, Knowsley.road, and Dunriding-lane to the field. The inspecting officer was accompanied by Captain Rigg, as aide-de-camp, and after the usual reception had been given a variety of movements were gone through. At the close of the inspection a hollow square was formed, and the inspect. ing officer addressing them said making my 'port, I shall be happy to make a vary satisfactory one, generally. I have seen what has been done in the shape of works, lilt it would be more satis- factory to me to see you do some of the bridging and the engineering work; but, of coarse, that was not poembiewith the limited time at our disposal. lam quite satisfied .with ithe bridging, and if one of the bridges did break dowif under the weight of one of the companies it was not your fault, t

Ibut the fault of the span. The colonel showed me the models made by some members of the corps, and some of them are very creditable indeed,—two or three,—and I should like afterwards to see the three men. With regard to your drill, you have not a very favourable piece of ground, and I cannot expect you to be quite so steady as you would be on parade, but altogether the movements are very fair. You do not keep quite good distances; you lost them by degrees. The volunteers I have noticed do some things just as well ,as the regulars themselves, because in- telligence is common to all, and there may be some things they can dO better—as for instance some of the men of Sir William Armstrong's factory can mann a gun quicker by half a minute, than the old gunners of Shoebuty- ness. Of course, the object of your training is not to make you infantry, but still if you can work well together, and steadily, you will be altogether better sappers. Of course, ' there are times when the sappers fight like the infantry. I repeat again, that I shall make a satisfictory report of you to the general.—On the field were Captain Calrow, R.E., adjutant of the Ist L.E.V., and captain of the Ist Royal Engineers; Lieut.-Colonel J. Roth well, commanding; Major , T. C. Wilcock, Captain and Adjutant P. Curry, Surgeon IL F. Hall, M.D., Captains, Ward, Duffy, ifigg, Campbell, and T Craik ; Lieutenants Massey, Brooker, M`Kechnie Moncrieff, rendlebary, Crooks, Dee, and Lyon; Sergeant-M'ajor Burns, R.E., and Sergeant Instructor Goss, R.E. Field state— present on parade ; 15 officers, 24 sergeants, 29 band and buglers, and 365 rank and file—total, 453. Absent with leave: four officers, three sergeants, one bandsman, and 58 I Yank and file--total, 65. The full strength of the corps is 498. The regiment afterwards marched through the town and back to the Engineer Hall, where each member received 6d. in lieu of refreshments. They then dispersed.

A Darban telegram states that the Royal Commission has framed a convention containing 36 articles, and that the Boers have rejected 16 of these. The Standard correspon- dent at Durban states•on the authority of telegrams from Pretoria that the terms of the convention as settled by the Commission give to the Boers the right to *.lect a Volksraad and President. Phe treaty reserves to the Suzerain the right of declaring war. The whole of the Transvaal is to be returnedto the Boers, the proviso as to a belt on the eastern side having been abandon.d. No British subjects are to be subject to military service. A long period is allowed for the payment of State debts. Sir Evelyn Wood leaves shortly for Zululand.

PROPOSED GREAT LIBERAL BANQUET.—A movement is on foot to invite Mr. GI akone and the members of his Cabinet to a public dinner at tbe Crystal Palace, "to express to him and them the grateful sense entertained by the people of England of the policy of peace, progress, retrenchment, and freedom at home and abroad which has characterised their retention of office, and to show that he and they may folly rely upon the earnest support of all sections of the Liberal party in their present and future efforts to reform all abuses arid further without delay the great end of all legislation—. the greatest happiness of the greatest number, the sole aim of the Liberal party." It is possible that after the labours of a Litigoing session the Ministry may not accept the invitation, bat nothing has yet been decided in the matter.

Tan Bread' Reform League, which is now'in ful I ',operation, appears likely to effect a change in the manner of making the .great household requisite, bread. The:League has secured Ur. Samuel Morley for its president, and the fDuchess of Sutherland, the Earl of Shaftesbury, and the Rev. Cancm'Duckworth are on the list of patrons. Among the vice-presidents we notice the names of Dr. Beddoe, Dr. Carpenter, Professor Rae Lancaster, Dr. Richardson,-Sir Thomas Watson, and Professor Erasmus Wilson. It sliciuld be remembered that the League is not a commercial undertaking. It aims at introducing pure, whole- some, nutritious bread made from wheat meal, 'pro- perly prepared, in place of the white breed, which is deprived of much of its notirishing and sustaining quality. Miss Yates, who is the originator of the movement, has succeeded in winning influential sup- port, and makes a strong appeal to the public to try brown bread as it -can now be prepared. She has observed that an old English revival has -set in, and we are surrounded by mediceval arOlaitecture, antique furniture, and brown and yellow coloured lace and drapery, and she asksms to carry the movement a step further, and bring into fashion good old English brown bread, which will have the practical advan- tage of bringing health and strength to -many a humble home. Brown, as compared with white, is, she says,- always symbolical of strength, or power, whilst white is typical of weakness or immaturity. Brown -80a8 are always more fertile than light sandy or chalky soils. Brown or dark coloured meats are more nourishing than white flesh or fish. The whiter the bread the less nourishment it contains. In fact, the whitenese.of the tread may be considered an outward sign of the starvation within. Miss , Yates is sure that those who give good brown wheat meal bread a fair trial 'will find it nourishes and sus- tains them better than white bread does, and that a larger amount of work can be done on it alone than on white bread alone, and that, all other things being equal, the nation which is fed principally on good brown bread will be superior to the nation which is fed principally on white bread.

AT a period when the thermometer is in this country registering 98 in the shade, we should think that the very thought of wearing woollen materials, English made or others, seems burdensome and oppreseive. And yet we find people are calling attention just now I to an association that has lately been formed by a , number of ladies, for the most part titled,. for en- couraging the use of English woollen manufactures, in preference to those of foreign make. The sympathy, if not the judgment, of most English people, will go with the association in their well- meant effort for the encouragement of native industry. Whether this plan responds to the sound economic principle that the wants of a community shauld be satisfied whencesoever satisfaction can be had at the smallest outlay, we will not stay to ingnire. The ladies' aosociation, who have probably been carried forward by good motives rather than by good reasons, are seemly likely to have thought much upon such points as this. They, no doubt, I mean well, and that will be enough to earn them a 1 certain amount of admiration. It seems to be of little moment to the Indio who have undertaken to apply a corrective to the wrongs arising out of oar modern economic arrangements, that the only protec- tion which they are likely to extend to the native woollen manufacture, will effect the very class of other whichna t nations. niss. lealstt airsecntoetd btyhetheblsecral markets by prohibitiveB English woollen good heavier goods which the duchesses and marchionesses and countesses who patronise the association, cannot taritha.itt zrehuktepttheonethoefapeplofalieifeYairoodff possibly wear.

LOCAL NOTES.

"Where ignorance is bliss, 'tis folly to be wise," especially with regard to dietary matters. Just now as we are all parched with thirst we are admonished by some medical men to eschew liquid refreshment of every sort. Even a draught of the cool spring or sparkling rill, BO beloved by the poet, may exert a baneful effect upon our constitution. To take alcohol in, any form is to court apoplexy, while in- dulgence in a glass of iced lemonade is equivalent to furnish- ing tie family undertaker with an order. We ask for some- thing to drink and are told that we may partake very moderately of tea or coffee, and even then our immunity from danger is only problematic. Then with, shall I say, heartless cunning the last straw Is laid upon the camel's back. We are informed that these bevetages will probably render us more thirsty and hot than before we indulged in them. Under such circumstances the question whether life is worth living becomes more unanswerable than ever. How sad must have been the condition of our unenlightened forefathers, who, when thirsty, drink heartily of whatever beverage they fancied, without, for a moment, „questioning the deleterious influence it might have upon them. 1 would j

add, however, that there ate a number of doctors who tell us we should be unsparing in our consumption of un-iced and non-stimulating liquids; and when doctors disagree who shall decide?

I learn that the Prescot School Board have resolved to try and solve the difficulty of dealing with the arrears (I schools by ordering the teachers to refuse admission to those children who did not bring the current fee. Now I scarcey think that this course is in accordance with the spirit of the Education Act. School Boards have been brought io existence for the express purpose of seeing that every thild receives a good sound elementary education, and if tbe pree- cot School Board desire to do their duty they must not refuse admission to their school to any chile.. When a parent can pay the school fees of his children, and will not do so, he ought to be compelled; but when the School Board decide to refuse admission to the children they are depriving those little ones of the education they would otherwise receive. True the Board may afterwards summon the parents for not sending their children to school, but I fear that -ender such circumstances they will find some difficulty in convicting the parents, and even if they succeed 'the children will never be able to make up for the time that has I been lost by their being sent back by the school authorities. I certainly think that the better plan under the present law would have been for the Board to admit the children and take proceedings to recover the fees, although I must con- fess that I see a great deal of force in the argument put for- ward by many workingmen and others—that since the State compels the children to attend school for the benefit of the State, the latter ought to pay for the education. Amongst most people our soldiers have the reputation of being a careless improvident set of dogs who would save no- thing if they could, and could save nothing if they would. That this estimate of our country's defenders is based more upon imagination than fact is agreeably illustrated by some statistics recently published, which show that on a certain day this year a sum of nearly £300,000, was due to deposi- tors in the various military savings' banks. No doubt such a statement will be a surprising revelation to the majority of people, and will probably lead them to give the soldier credit for mote wisdom and self denial than he has hitherto been considered capable of manifesting.

' There is a good deal of talk just now about the new comet which itsaid will shortly be seen in this country. If, as some peop)e imagine, we are really indebted to the co.net for the tremendous heat we are enduring, the news that another of these erratic visitants is approaching us will scarcely be welcome to t hoes who object to 90 degrees in the shade. There is however a crumb of comfort in the hope that the Yankee astronomers like the Yankee prophets are out of their calculations this time. We don't want to be scorched up to a cinder just yet. •

• I expect that we shall soon begin to regard the weather prophets with a little suspicion. The New York Herald 'storm warning has somehow "gone wrong" and the frirrecasts from the meteorological department have for several day 8 past been singularly misleading. Several hurricanes thunderstorms, and pleasant showers have gone astray some- ' where.

Mr. Annett, the master of Trinity Boys' School. Run corn, with whom the School Board have lately Lad a very pretty little quarrel, has proved remarkably successful in the Government examination before Her Majesty's 'nspe ctor, having passed 94 per cent of his scnolors ! What will Mr. John Simpson say to this ? Several of the friends of the Trinity school master say that he is quite right in the view which be has taken of his duties as to the School Board, an! that the appeal of the -..,mbers of that body to the Education Department will an end in smoke. The Widnes Local Board have taken a new departure in deciding to appoint Mr. Allen, a gentleman who also acts ae their accountant, to tbeposition of lay clerk in the place of Mr. Thomas Beasley, who filled both the offices of law and ordinary clerk, and had been connected with the Board for about 15 3 ears. DnionvErr AT DITTON. INTERESTING TO ANTI. QuAlss.—During the past few weeks Mr. E. Timmins, of the Bridgewater Foundry, has been engaged sinking on the siteof the artesian well on the south side of Ditton station, •upon land belonging belonging to the London and North- 'Western Railway Company. On Friday week, as the men were boring they discovered an earthenware jug, about 12 feet from the surface, in the alluvium strata. On being brought to the top, it was found to be quite sound. It had apperently been made wholly by hand, and'bore fingermark impressions. There are a few marks upon the jug which are thought to be a date of 1711 or 1411. Two or three centuries ago a castle, or monastery, stood near the spot where the well it being sunk. The jug has been sent by Mr. Timmins to Mr. F. W. Webb, the engineer of the railway tompany, Crewe. On 'Wednesday, two Roman coins, of re- rnarkable pure copper, were found at thosame place. They have Latin inscriptions upon them. - -

TRINITY CHURCH ' CHOIR, I:Wl.4cm-tr.—The choir con- nected with Trinity Church have just had their annual pic-nic. The place chosen this year was the Overton Hills, whither the party went in vehicles by road, and a most en. joyable time was spent. An excellent tea was provided by Mr. Rigby, of Belle Monte. The ;chairman, the Rev. W. Preston, inhis remarks afterwards, said he was pleased to be able to say 'that they all had worked together well and har- moniously for the past twelve months. He hoped that no jarring digcord would intrude itself into their midst, but that they would continue to acttogether and work harmoniously, not to please man, or to gain human applause, but for the glory of God and for the honour of His name; doing what they performed as a work for Him. He hoped that this would be the stimulating motive of all that they under- took; and so acting they would be blessed. •For his own part and in behalf of the congregation he thanked them heartily for the help they rendered in conducting the worship of Almighty Ga. Mr. Churchwarden Buckley was amongst those Who accompanied the party.

THE CHATSWORTH OF LANCASHIRE.—The sixth grand exhibition of plants and flowers in connection with the Waterloo, Seaforth and Crosby Floral and Horticultural Society was held on Wednesday last, in the conservatories and grounds of the International Marine Hvdropathic Com- pany, Limited, &afield-on-the-Mersey. The directors of the company courteously invited all the members of the Wesleyan Methodist Conference, which is now Meeting in „Liverpool, to be present, with their wives, an epportunity which was largely availed of. The number of 'spectators exceeded all former meetings. The show was opened by Councillor Anthony Bower, J.P., who, in referring to the interest called forth by this exhibition, said: I think, also, that our pleasure is all the more that the various specimens can be inspected, wherp they appear to such advantage, as in the magnificent range of conservatories in which we are I now assembled. These conservatories are planned so that in walking along any part of the principal quadrangle the whole square is constantly in view. This, with the flowers within showing through the glasses, the vines in full bear- ing, and the fountains playing, makes the sight one of sur- passing interest and unrivalled beauty, and I think you will agree with rne that the series, as a whole, is so extensive and complete, it is no exaggeration to claim for it that it is the "Chatsworth of Lancashire." The establishment, which is very large, is being prepared as one of the finest Marine Hydropathic Establishments in the kingdom, and is to be opened for visitors early next spring.

FLownn SERVICE AT RUNCORN.—Tne first flower service which has been held in Runcorn took place on Sun- day evening at Bethesda Congregational chapel. We see by a modern writer that flowers have always been an emblem of purity; and this idea has long been recognised, in varied forms, by the Christian Church. Several plants and flowers were connected by our ancestors with certain saints on account .of their coming into bloom about the time of the recurrence of certain saints' days. Thus the snowdrop was called the purification flower, as it blossomed about Candle- mas; the crocus was dedicated to St. Valentine; the daisy to St. Margaret; the cardamine, or lady's smock, to the virgin, its white flowers appearing about Lady Day; and the St. John's wort, as its name implies, with the disciple whom Jesus loved. The rose, which justly earned the title of queen of flowers, was said to fade about St. Magdalen's Day. There were also the Lent lily, or daffodil, the pasque flower, or anemone, herb Trinity, limb Christopher, St. Bar- naby's thistle, herb St. Robert, and Mary Wert. We con- gratulate the good folks of Bethesda on the manner in which they carried' out their promise of a flower service in the pleasant month of July, for what more appropriate than that the " anemones that spangle every grove, the primrose wan, and harebell mildly blue," with the infinite variety of flowers which adorn our gardens and hothbuses, should be used to adorn the place where Jehovah is worehipped, who, in the person of His incarnate Son, told us to consider the lilies how they grow, for Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed in such beauty as these. On visiting the chapel on Sunday evening we found that great pains had been bestowed to make it as 'beautiful as possible, and every available niche and corner was ornamented with some of the prettiest flowers of the season. The communion table and rails were specially worth of notice. Round the gallery were hung festoons of plants, and bouquets to the number of about 120 were placed in various parts of the edifice. Most of the friends present wore buttonholes. The Rev. J. D. Thomas, the pastor, ho appears to be very popular with the people, preached an appropriate discourse, and suitable hymns were sung by the choir.

'The Registrar of Friendly Societies calls attention to the official memorandum on valuations of friendly societies, in which it is pointed out that the Friendly Societies Act, 1875, requires all societies to return to him a valuation once at least in every five years. RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT LYTHAIL—An accident occurred at Lytham on Wednesday afternoon to a passenger train pre- ceding to East Lancashire. A large piece of wood had been left on the rails about a mile from the station, where some repairs are going on, and this threw the tram of the metals. The train travelle3 in this way for nearly 100 yards, when it regained them. Until informed of the accident, the pas- sengers were unaware of its occurrence. Much damage was done to the line, and the engine also suffered. The driver of the train was the man Bulfield, who so narrowly escaped in the Burscough collision. A LAMB ASSAULTING • LLIES AT NORTHWICEL—At the Northwich Police Court, on Saturday, before Mr. Neu- mann, James Lamb, flstrnan, Leicester-street, was charged with assaulting his wife. Complainant, whose head was bandaged and appeared much bruised, said that about ten o'clock on Friday night defendant came home, went up stairs, and soon came down again, when he asked her for some water. Immediately afterwards he seized a chair and struck her about the head with it, severely cutting her. Corroborative evidence was given by the complainant's daughter. FALL FROM • RAILWAY BRIDOE AT WARRINGTON.— An accident of a somewhat serious character occurred on Sunday, to a boy named Thomas Hewitt, seven years of age, and whose parents reside at 96, Pierpoint-street, Warrington. The boy, it is stated, was ascending the steps which lead from the railway to Bewsey Bridge, when be missed his footing, and fell a distance of about 12 feet. Fortunately he was found a few minutes later by a man on the railway, lying across the metals. He was bleeuing from a wound on the forehead, and was completely insensible. He was at once conveyed to the Infirmary, where every attention Was paid him, but he continued unconscious until Monday morning. Ile has received some injury to the spine, and though progressing very favourably, he is not yet considered out of danger. REMARKABLE FREAK OF NATURE AT CIIERDLEY.—A remarkable freak of nature is now to be seen at the house of Mr. A. Gray, shepherd, Cuerdley. It seems that Mr. Gray had sent a sitting of Brahma eggs to his son, Mr. J. Gray, Widnes, which turned out very successful. One of the eggs was not quite hatched, and Mrs. Gray, thinking it was a bad one, to satisfy herself she broke the shell, when to her surprise she saw a full developed chicken with four legs, the two fore legs being where the wings should be. The house has been visited by a large number of people during the week. It might be said that a few months ago another instance nearly of the same nature occurred at the neigh- bouring farm of Mr. Moorecroft, which was a chicken with four wings. It is a pity that they were not allowed to be properly hatched, as then they would have been more re- markable. - A PARLIAWENTittY COMET.—At a recent meeting at Chelsea to discuss the Irish Land Bill, Mr. Firth, M.P., re- ferring to Lord Randolph Churchill's Parliamentary career, said:. The noble lord pursues in Parliament a course almost as elliptical and erratic as the comet which has been visiting us lately. Nor is this the only point of resemblance between the two. Astronomer tells ne that the heavenly comet is entirely without substance; is mainly composed of gas; and is of a levity inconc-ivable to ordinary mortals So with the Parliamentary comet. Judged by his public utterances, no one credits him with the possession of much substance; he is mainly composed of gas, and is of a levity quite inconceivable to those who are outside the walls of Parliament. In one point, however, they unfortunately differ. Ido not question that both may have a heavenly origin, but we are told that the heavenly comet is speeding rapidly from the space we inhabit, to be seen of the teen of this generation no more. Would that we might say the same of the Parliamentary comet?

RESIGNATION OF THE CHIEF CONSTABLE OF LIVERPOOL. —After close on 30 years' local service, Major Greig, C. 8., chief of the city constabulary, has sent in his resignation. "The Major" (then Captain Greig) received his appoint- -1 iment in 1852, being elected in succession to Mr. Dowling. who was successor to Mr. Michael James Whitty. His salary, commencing at £5OO a year with house rent, has grown with the growth of his duties to £l,OOO a year, with £5O for the keep of a horse and £lO2 for rent and taxes. His first increase was made on the 31st March, 1855, when his salary was raised to £650 a year. On the 20th March, 1860, it was further increased by £100; and again on the 21st, 1865, by a further £lOO, making it £B5O. Finally, in May, 1868, the Major's salary was raised to the amount at which it now stands. Besides this income he has for some years received a percentage from the superannuation fund. Thus altogether he receives from £1,200 to £1,300 a year; and his retiring allowance will probibly be about £650 per annum. During his period of office also be received military promotion, while his services in connection with the Fenian descent on Chester, in February, 1867, were re- cognised by the conferment of a Civil Companionship of the Order of the Bath.

WARRTNOTON CATTLE AND HORSE FAIR. —Owing to tbe 17th July falling on Sunday this year, the annual cattle and horse fair was held on Monday and Tuesday last in Winwick-street, from the Central Station to Town's End. Usually, the first day is set apart for cattle, but there were also a large number of horses and colts present at the fair on that day. Though, perhaps, not equal in numbers to previous years, the cattle were of averaee quality, the Eng- lish much cows being especially good. There were also some fair specimens of Irish heifers, a large proportion, in fact, of the 250 animals estimated to be present being of that class. The day being fine the fair was thronged, but business was rather quiet, and comparatively little money changed hands. Mulch cows commanded prices ranging from 15s. to 255., and almost all the animals of this class were sold. Heifers, however, appearee to be little in demand, and but few offers were made, the slowness of the sale being manifest by the numbers present on the following day. The horse fair commenced at ten o'clock on Tuesday morning, and continued until about seven o'clock in the evening. It was considerably more crowded than on the previous day. The number of horses for sale was very large, and a larger space had to be allowed for the purposes of the fair. From £5O to £7O were asked for good d-aught horses, but few animals changed hands. There was a number of useful colts on sale, but they did not find many buyers. On the whole, we think the fair was equal to for- mer years. •
DEPUTATION OF WARRINGTON AND BIRMINGHAM LIBERALS TO HAWARDEN.

1 A deputation of Birmingham Liberals, numbering about 50, from the Birmingham Forward Liberal Club, visited Hawarden, on Monday, to present a me.norial to Mr. Glad- e ne. A party of 28 Liberals, including several ladies, also left Bank Quay station at 10 a.m. for Chester, thence pro- ceeding in two conveyances to Hawarden Here they joined the Birmingham deputation, and at the 'request of Mr. Norman, Messrs. Plumpton, Critchley, Siddell, and him- self, were allowed to form part of the deputation which had to present the address. In the -bsence sf Mr. Gladstone, who was unable to leave his Parliamentary duties, his son, the Rev. Stephen Gladstone, received the deputation. Mr. Wright, of Birmingham, presented the memorial in a suit- able speech. It was as follow : To the Right Honourable W. E. Gladstone, M.P., First Lord of Her Majesty's Treasury. Sir,—On behalf of the Birmingham Forward Liberal I Club, an Association of six hundred persons, mainly 1 belonging to the artizan class, we desire to present to you 1 this formal expression of our thanks for the permission you have kindly given us to visit Hawarden Castle and Park; a locality which, independently of its natural beauties, has for us, and for all Liberals throughout the country, a personal and historic interest, in being the home of one whom we are proud to acknowledge as the foremost of Eng- lish Statesmen.

In offering our thanks for your kindness, you will how- ever understand that the expression of them is much more than a mere matter of form. Coming from a body of Bir- mingham men, the feeling we desire to convey to you cannot indeed be otherwise than deep and sincere; a feeling of gratitude of trust, and of admiration ; of gratitude for the great and prolonged service you have rendered to your country; of trust, in the principles by which you are animated, in the policy which you advocate, and in the nobility, the devotion, and the purity of your personal character; and of admiration of the determined effc.rts you are now making to carry a great measure of justice to the cultivators of the soil in Ireland.

we reflect with satisfaction and with pride upon the loyal and undeviating support which Birmigham has given to the Liberal measures which you have from time to time brought forward, and to the patriotic and beneficient policy of which you are the chief exponent and advocate; we rejoice that in the persons of two of our trusted and honoured representa- tives who are your colleagues in the Government we are enabled to render you efficient support in upholding Liberal principles, and in promoting Liberal policy; and We fervently hope that your health and strength may be main- tained, so that you may triumphantly complete the great work you now have in hand, and may be able in the future to render services worthy to stand beside those which al- ready confer impenshable honour upon your name, and have ensured to you the lasting appreciation and gratitudeof your countrymen. Renewing our thanks for the kindness you have shown us to-day,--I have the honour to be, on behalf of the "Forward Club," Your faithful Servant, WILLILM COOKE, Chairman. In accepting the memorial on behalf of his father, the Rev. S. Gladstone thanked the deputation for their visit, which he was sure his father would appreciate. The depu- tation were shown through the grounds, and a very pleasant day was spent, the Warrington Liberals arriving home about nine o'clock p.m.

div.head: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN,
div.p: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN,

- HOPB OF EARLESTOWN LODOE.—At the usual weekly session of the above lodge, on Mondsy, after the routine business, four candidates were admitted to member- ship. Bro. J. W. Hall, C. Deputy, and Bro. Jno. Taylor, of Warrington, who were present as visitors, were heartily re- ceived. Arrangements were made for a fraternal visit from ' the Warrington Temperance Mission Lodge. A pleasant and I instructive entertainment by various members followed. On Wednesday evening about 18 members of the Hope of Earleetown Lodge of Good Tempters left Earlestown by train for Leigh, to assist the Leigh Alpha Lodge in holding an open air meeting. The whole party of members and visitors left the Leigh lodge-room at 7-30, and proceeded to the Market-place, where an audience of about 200 persons assembled, who listened most attentively to Mr. M. Dull, of Manchestsr, occasional lecturer for the United Kingdom Alliance. A vote of thanks to chairman and lecturer having been adopted, the members and visitors returned to the lodge-room, where a coffee supper was prepared for them. A most enjoyable evening was spent. MELANCHOLY DEATH OF MR. JOSIAH HADFIELD EVANS. —On Sunday last intelligence was received at Haydock of the sudden death of Mr. Josiah Hadfield Evans, son of the late Mr. Josiah Evans, of Haydock. The deceased gentle- man was only twenty-three years of age, and has not been married more than a year. About a fortnight ago, in com- pany with one of his sisters, Miss Kate Evans, who resides at Haydock, he went for a short tour tO Norway. On Satur- day last a telegram was received in Manchester stating that he had been drowned off the coast of Norway, but that his sister, Miss Evans, was safe. No further details have yet came to hand, but it is supposed that he must have been drowned while creasing in a small boat from the Norwegian coast to one of the small islands with which it is fringed. Mr. Hadfield Evans was the nephew of Mr. Joseph Evan the colliery proprietor, of Haydock, and the grandson of Mr. Hadfield, the late M.P. for Sheffield. The news of his melan- choly death has been received in Haydock with a feeling ef general regret. He was well known and greatly respected io the locality, where he for many years lived, and where the home of his mother, Mrs. Evans, now is.
LATEST NEWS.
THE WIMBLEDON MEETING.

-The Olympic Pi ize, in reference to which the disclosures of last year arose, has been won by Lieutenant-Masao, of the Ist Renfrew, with 70 points; Sergeant West, of St. Helens, made 36 points. The Heath Prize returns haws been issued, this morning. Corporal Hart, let Warwick, Lieutenant Heap, 6th Lancashire, and Private Wallace, iltk Lanalls, each take £7 13s. 4d. with 35 points, and Private Griffiths, 17th Lancashire, gets £3 with 34. In the Robin Hood series Sergeant Smith, 3rd Cheshire, earns £3; Cor- poral Perry, 19th Lancashire £3.: Private Lewis, 2nrl Cheshire, £2. Lieutenant Woolley, 2nd Cheshire, gets 412 in the Wills competition, and a similar sum is awarded t• Colour-Sergeant Smith, 3rd Cheshire. In the Permanent staff contest, Sergeant Wallace, Ist Cheshire, secured £1 with a score of 23.

wAsHINGTox, F. iday.—President Garfield's condition continues favourable. A fragment of clothing passed from the President's wotaid, yesterday, through the proocerof supplication.
GREAT FIRE. BORDEAUX, Thursday.lo p.m.—A fire broke out here this evening in a large wive warehouse. Eight thousand casks of wine have already been destroyed, and the conflagration IC still raging.

THE WESLEYAN CONFERENCE. Proceedings were resumed on Thursday; the Rev. Dr. Osborne, president, in the chair. The Rev. Benjamin Hellier, at the instance of several old students present, asked the sanction of the conference for permission to raise funds to found a scholarship at Headingley College, Leeds, to per- petuate the memory of the late Rev. Samuel Coley. He had reason to believe that such a memorial would aieet with generous support from ministers and Methodist laymen in all parts of the connexion. In reply to Mr. Bond it was stated that the proposed scholarship would be confined to students at Headingley College. Sanction was accordingly given. The conference then proceeded to the further con- sideration of ministerial character. In this matter the utmost privacy is observed, which is equalled only by the fidelity with which the subject is investigated. A letter WAS read from the Rev. James Brooke, of Manchester, who is the oldest living Wesleyan minister, lie is in his 93rd year, and desired to express his abiding affection for his brethren. A suitable reply was sent.

Mr. Bradlaugh has been advised that payment of £2OO, and execution of indemnity bond by Mr. Newdigate to Mr. Henry Lewis Clark, renders Mr. Newdegate liable to pro ceedings for maintenance, and Mr. Bradlaugh states he in- tends to sue that gentleman for damages to cover the whole of the expenses to which be has been out. According to Russel on Crimes, a person is guilty of maintenance who shall provide money, or otherwise aid in the prosecution of a suit to which be is not personally a party. Punishment is fine and imprisonment, in addition to chil damages. The case of Bradlaugh v. Clarke was concluded in Queen's Bench to-day. The learned judge in summing up, poiated out that the issue was simply whether Mr. Brad- laugh had voted before the writ in the action was issued or afterwards. The jury after one hour and three quarters deliberation found for the plaintiff.
The Cabinet Council summoned for to-day will be held twt noon.

Another knife has been found on the Brighton Railway near the scene of Mr. Gold's murder. It is an ordinary desert knife, but bears no resemblance to the cutlery used at prisoner's Wallington lodgings. It is now definitely decided that the funeral of the Dean of Westminster shall take place at four o'clock on Monday next, this hour having been appointed in order to suit the convenience of the Prince of Wales. The boys of West- minster school will follow the remains of the dean to the grave, but beyond this there will be no other public demon • stration.
The fourteen days' notice given by pony drivers at Denaby Main Colliery, one of the largest in South Yorkshire, ex- pired on Thursday, and as a consequence 1,000 men and boys are thrown out of work.

At a meeting at Oldbury, on Thursday, of nailers' dele- gates representing operatives in the Staffordshire and War- wickshire districts, who have for months been on strike for an advance of 30 per cent in wages, it was resolved to re- duce the demand to 20 per cent., and it is now thought a settlement of the dispute may be effected.

NATIONAL LIBEIW, FEDERATION.—At a meeting of the committee of tha National Liberal Federation on Thursday, at Birmingham, a resolution was passed expressing satisfac- tion at the progress of the Irish Land Bill, as amended and improved by the House of Commons, and appointing an emergency committee to watch it. JUT ther progress, with a view to secure its becoming law. It was decided to hold the next annual meeting at Liverpool, in the antumn, and to bold a series of conferences and meetings in various towns. A resolution was also passed urging the constituencies to 1.043 their influence to secure the admission of the junior member for Northampton to his seat in Parliament.

At the meeting of the Wesleyan Conference on Thursday, the Rev. C. Garrett stated that he had received a letter from Mr. A. Balfour, announcing his desire to contribute £lOO towards the expenses of the Conference. Severxl members spoke in appreciation of this gift. The review of the death- roll of the year was then continued.

HOUSE OF LORDS.

Lord WATENET brought in a Bill to provide improved dwellings for cottier tenants in Ireland and Boothia. The Bill was read a first time.—The Indicature Bill was read a third time and passed, and their Lordships adjourned.
