TEE COMMESCIAL TREATY WITH SPAIN.—Sit C. DILEF said the negotiation between England and Spain with re- gard to the Commercial Treaty had not progressed suffi- ciently to enable papers to be produced before prorogation. ENDOWED SCOTTISH INSTITUTIONS.— Mr. GLADSTONE said be could net withdraw the orders laid on the table dealing with endowed institutions in Scotland. MIDHAT Pecna..—Sir C. Dir.xs said Government had no intelligence from Turkey relative to fate of Midbat Pacha for the last 48 houre. Mr. Coax, in order to save that eminent man from death moved, the adjournment, of the House in order that a discussion might take place which he believed would have an effect at Constantinople. Be severely commented on the trial.---Mr. GI ADSTONE regretted the remarks of the hon. member. Right of inter- vention we had none, but as late as the fourth of July Lord Dufferin had done his utmost to induce the Sultan to pursue a lenient and considerate course, believing such would give satisfaction to enlightened opinion in Europe, and greatly conduce to the interests of the Sultan himself. Tux IRISH LAND BILL.—The Hpuse went into Commit- tee on the Irish Land Bill. A new clause, moved by Mr. GLADSTONE, providinn for audit of the accounts of the land commission was agreed to.—Mr. FirremacK moved a new clause providing that the landlords should, with the consent of the court, receive out of the purchase money any sum paid by him or his predecessor in title for the purchase of any right of sale of the tenants interest in the holding.— After some discussion, the clause was rejected by= to 78. Sir G. CAMPBELL moved a clause to secure continuity of tenancy, but it was not pressed. Several new clauses were ruled out of order.—Mr. RICHARD Powart moved a new clause to enable a tenant to make certain deductions in case of an absentee landlord.—Mr. GLADSTONE objected to the clause as likely to lead to all sorts of difficulty.—A long dis- cussion ensued, and on a division, there were for the clause 40; against, 249.—Mr. PARNELL had a cluse anthorising the court refusing refusing the application of an absentee landlord to fix fair rent of holding of tenant, but the Chair- man said that after the divibion just taken it could not be put —Mr. MARTIII then moved a new clause for encouraging the planting of timber trees and for extending the provisionsuner Of the special act of sth Geo. 3rd, chap. 17, and 6th Geo. 3rd, chap. 20, to every tenant of a present tenancy d the present Bill.—The krronxxv-Gzsmatit for IRELAND objected to the clause. A long discussion ensued, but the clause was withdrawn. Mr. CHAPLIN then moved a clause for providing that there should be laid before both Houses of Parliament return showing the judicial amount fixed in every court or by land commission, showing whether the same equal to or less than or greater than the rent payable by the ten int at the date when the application was made, and where it was greater or less than former rent, and also the circumstances and reasons for increases or reductions made by court or commission.—Mr. GrAnsToNE opposed. The clause would do more harm than good.—Mr. CILarIAIN expressed his willingness to omit the latter part of the clause after the word made."—Mr. Butotrr showed the difficulty the clause would create without the slightest nacessity.—Lord R. CHURCHILL and others supported the clause.--For the clause, 98 ; against, HI. [LEFT SITTING.]

THE WARRINGTON DEPUTATION TO THE LORDS OF TER Commrrritz or PRIVY COUNCIL.—The School Board Chronicle commenting on the interview which took place between the deputation from Lancashire and Cheshire lock authorities, and Mr. Mundella says:—" The figure made by Warrington was amusing. We have often had occasion to comment upon the absurd, the prejudiced and the discredit- able position which the town of Warrington occupies in connection with the great work of national education, but we did not expect that members of the Warrington Town Council would be so innocent as to air their benighted notions and prejudices before the authorities at Whitehall Mr. Mundella, as a matter of course, bad a very ehoi answer for the foolish suggestion that power should be placed in the hands of the Warrington Town Council to build Board schools. He told them to apply for an order, for the election of a School Board,*and he threatened t, cu: off the grant ef any school in Warrington which ref u. take in the poorer clasa of children."

------ STARR-BOWEEFT BUILDING SOCIETIES. one who has joined a Starr-Bowkett Building Society I must confels to some amount of interest in the letters which have recently appeared in yourcolumns op the subject. Ido not think that the reply given by Mt. Starr to his Warrington friends can be said to be characterised ley a spirit of frankness. Why does he not boldly and fearlessly deny the insinuations conveyed by the questions put to him at the Runcorn meeting and in The Examiner if there is no foundation for them ? If the principles by which these societies are guided are good, and the societies are being established for the benefit of the members and for that of certain individuals, no person can say but that the more the matter is discussed the better. Let Mr. Starr answer fairly• and plainly the questions put to him, or if he will not, then let him tell us the reason why. In the absence of this, I and many other members will begin to think that tbere:is a strong reason in the background.—Yours truly, Runcorn, July 16th, 1881 A MEMBER.
THE GOOD TEMPLAR CHARTER SUIT.

TEMPERLIPCE V. LITIGATION. Sir,—ln the "Good Templars' Watchword" of Rine 20th and 27th, 1881, giving an account of the proceedings before Use Referee in the suit Lees v. MalMs, I find in the opening address of the counsel for the plaintiff, that at the .session of the R.W.G.L. held at Bloomington, Illinois, U.S.A., in 1875, coloured representatives were admitted ; also that Mr. Matins and Dr. Lees, who attended that meeting as repre- sentatives of from the Grand Lodge of England, were highly delighted to sit there in council with their coloured brethren. Again, at the Newcastle session of the Grand Lodge of England, held at Easter, 1876, Mr. Malins and Dr,. Lees (among others) were elected as representatives to the session of the R.W.U.L. held at Louisville, Kentucky, in May, 1876, and duly attended it; and it was at this meeting that a division in the membership took place, on the so- called negro " question, that Mr. Malins with several others left the session, and, proceeding to the Masonic Hall, formed what is now called the R.W.G.L. of the world, giving as a reason for eo doing that the R.W.G.L. hail violated its prin- ciples by excluding the nem) from membership in it. Now, I simply ask if this can ''be so, when we are told that coloured representatives attended at Bloomington in 1875. I am afraid that Good Templars in general, and the Grand Lodge of England in particular, have been entirely misled upon this question; and from a very careful reading of the matter brought before the referee, and what has come to rov knowledge, as also from personal observition since the separation, I have arrived at the conclusion that it is simply a persooal question as between Mr. Malins and'Dr. Lees which shall be the G.W.C.T. of the Grand Lodge elf England, and that the." Negro" question has only been mud as a pretext to keep up the division that is still going on in the order. Again from the fact that Mr. Matins was elected as the G.W.C.T. of the Grand Lodge of England in 1870, and has been re elected from year to year up to the present time,l consider him as G.W.C.T., and that the meet- ing called by Colonel Hickman, in Manchester, in 1876, and at which Dr. Lees was elected as G.W.C.T., was enfirely illegal (because not called in accordance with the constitu- tion) therefore Dr. Lees cannot be the G.W.C.T., and ought , not to be recognised as such by any temperance organisa- tion. The same can apply to the supreme court of the order. The R.W.G.L. which was instituted in 1852, and has never dissolved or ceased to discharge its functions is sEIU the head of our order, whilst the R.W.G.L. ot the world insti- tuted in 1876 (being illegally constituted) has no locus- atandi. It appeares to me that the division in the order is merely a dispute between the Grand Lodge of England, and ths R.W.G.L., and the Charter Suit, a personal matter be- tween Mr. Matins and Dr. Lees, and that the same lies in a nutshell, all that is required being a reconciliation between the parties named, and which I hope to see brought about. The Grand Lodge of England in 1876, numbered about 130,000 members, while at the present time it numbers only 10,000, being a loss of 40,000. From £1,500 to £2,000 has been guaranteed to carry on this Charter Suit, whilst the (order is still declining both in member- ship and usefulness. How might the order have been increased, the temperance caused advanced, and many poor drunkard reclaimed if this money had been put to a more noble purpose. Ido sincerely hope our sub-lodges will look into this matter calmly, and urge upon the the several dis- trict authorities to convene a meeting of the members with an earnest desire to devise means in order that a reconcilia- tion may take place, so that instead of frittering away our energies and funds on a simple piece of paper called a charter, they may be devoted to the saving of the souls and bodies of the poor drnnkards . I dare to say that sub and district lodges were bastituted for this end, and my dear brethren go forward and carry out the blessed work you have set yourselves to do. Let temperance be your highest aim, and if the G.L. of England still desires to carry on this paper war, let them find their own funds by curtailing the salaries and expenses of its officers. lam a Good Tem- plar of 10 years standing, and have held several important positions connected therewith, and rather than leave it in its present low condition I am anxious to see it saved, because if allowed to go on as it is it will soon die out, in spite of what many of its most prominent members may say to the contrary. ONWARD IS OUR MOTTO.
PRESCOT SCHOOL BO A.RD.

The monthly meeting of the Prescot School Board was held on Monday, Mr. W. L. Evans, J.P., presiding. There were also present :—Hessre. Spencely, Wycherley, Sanders Goldsworth, and Brown ; with Mr. Henry Cross (clerk).

15EAVY FINE FOR DEFICIENCY OF TEACHING STAFF IN THE INFANT SCHOOL. The CLERK laid before the ,meeting the inspector's re- port of the midsernmer examination of the schools, which was as follows :—Boys' School : There has been much sick- ness during the past year in all departments of this school, and the teachers have had to labour with backward and neglected children who have been driven in from the streets. This a good deal explains the moderate attainments of the boys, and the poor examination passed by the first and se- wid standards. The writing on paper is good, but the third and fourth standards are very weak in spelling, and the lat- ter class failed in geography. The singing deserves much praise.—Girls' School: The girls have, all things considered, passed a creditable examination. The handwriting and spelling are good, and grammar has been well taught. Reading also, except in the first standard, is fluent, though rather wanting in intelligence. The firs'. and second standards will, I hope, next year be more advanced in arithmetic, and the girls generally do their sewing more ex- peditiously. the discipline is very satisfactory.—lnfants' Department • This department has deteriorated. The children are not iind,r control, and consequently the instruction however painstaking, has not been very effective. The six and five year old classes are backward. H.M. Inspector is unable to recommend the payment of the discipline grant to the infant's school. [This grant amounts to slightly ever £s.] The ilmount earned in Government grant was £229 153.84. against £240 183. Bd. earned last year, being a decrease of £ll 3s. From this amount (£239 15s. Bd.) has been deducted the sum of £2O inflicted as a fine fordeficiency of teaching staff in the infant school, leaving the total *mount to be received by the board, £209 15s. 80.—A die- cession took place respecting the fine, and it was eventually , resolved that the clerk write to the Education Department 1 asking for information on the point, and why the grant for ' the two pupil teachers had been withheld.—lt was resolved to advertise for two pupil teachers in their first or second year, one for the boys' school and the other for the girls' school.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY JULY 23, 1881.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY JULY 23, 1881.

BREACH OF THE PUBLIC HEALTH I ACT AT HIJYTON. At Prescot Sessions, on ,Tuesday, before Messrs. T. Pilkington and W. L. Evans Mr. William Henry Blain, of Liverpool and Huyton. was summoned at the instance of the Huyton-with-Roby Local • Board for commencing to erect certain buildings at Croft-house, Hnyton, before the plans of the same had been passed by the Board, and not giving notice to the surveyor when the erection of such buildings would be commenced.—Mr. W. Swift, clerk to the Local Board, prosecuted.—Defendant did not appear.—Mr. Evans : Is the defendant represented ?—Mr. Swift: No; not legally. This gentleman, who, I believe, is his archi- tect, appears for him, but I object to his taking part in the case for certain reasons.—The architect: We have .a full explanation of the case.—Mr. Evans: You can't appear for the defendant.—The architect: Then I ask that the case may be adjourned.—Mr. Swift: I saw defen- dant this morning, and he desired . the case to go on.—Mr. Swift, in opening the case, said that on the 25th April last defendant was intending to erect a coach-house, billiard-roem, and other buildings, and sent in plans to the Local Board about the 26th April. After quoting the section of the Public Health Act, giving powers to local boards to make bye-laws respecting the erection of new nuildings, structure of walls, ventilation, and drainage, the giving of notice, deposit of plans, dzc., Mr. Swift read section 158, which provided " that where a notice, plan, or description of any work is required by any bye-law made by any urban authority to be laid before that authority, the urban authority shall, within one month, after the same has been delivered, signify in writing their approval or dis- approval of the intended work to the person executing the same." Defendant, before waiting for the approval or dis- approval of the board, commenced within the space of a fortnight afterwards. He did not wait until the board had had a meeting to signify their approval or disapproval of the plans. Mr. Swift called the attention of the Bench to the 90th bye-law of the Local Board, which set forth that "Every per- son who shall intend to lay out or construct a street, or erect a building, or otherwise to execute any work to which any of these s relating to new streets and building shall apply, shall, before beginning to lay out oe construct such street, or erect such building, or execute such work, deliver or sent, or cause to be delivered or sent to the sur- veyor of the Sanitary Authority in writing, the date on which such person shall begin to lay out or construct such street, or erect such building, or execule such work." The corn- plaint of the Local Board was that the defendant having sent in plans, did not wait for the sanction of the Board, but be- gan to build, and began building without giving notice to the surveyor when the work would be commenced. For that offence defendant had rendered himself liable to a penalty of five pounds, and seeing that the defendant resided in the immediate neighbourhood and passed the office daily, he must ask their worships to inflict the full penalty. The Local Board were charged with the health of the district. and if gentlemen like Mr. Blain set their power 'And regulations at defiance there was no knowing what the result would be.—Joseph Worrell, surveyor to the Huy- ton-with-Roby Local Board, admitted having received plans Of proposed coach-house, billiard-room, and stables from the defendant on the 25th April. Defendant commenced to erect the buildings on the 16th May. At that time the plans had not been approved by the Board. Defendant did not give him any nodes in writing when he would corn- meqce the work. The buildings were about 150 feet from the road.—Mr. Evans: It appears he did not commence building till the 19th. What time should he have waited? —Mr. Swift: A month. And after that he must give notice to the surveyor of the Board when he is going to commence building, so that the surveyor may see that the buildings are put up in accordance with the plans submitted. With regard to the defendant having commenced building, if it was found that the buildings were not in accordance with the bye-laws, an order could be obtained for them to be pulled down.—ln reply to a remark by Mr. Evans, Mr. Swift stated that plane were usually considered by the High- way Committee, and there had been no meeting of that com- mittee between the-time the plans were submitted and the e next meeting of the Board. The Board did not entertain any plan before it had been before the Highway Committee. Mr. Blain lived close by the public offices, and h could have been made aware of it if he had made inquiry. The reason he asked for the maximum penalty to be inflicted was that it was a very small sum considering Mr. Blain's position and the gravity of the offence.—The magistrates, after a short consultation, inflicted a fine of SS and costs.

RAINFORD LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Monday evening, Mr. Howat presiding. There were also present— Messrs Agnew, John Birchall, Stockey, E. Birchall, Whalley, James Birchall, Boardman, Greener, Henry Webster, and J. K. Rosbotham.

GENERAL PERFUME COMMTELEE. At a meeting of the General Purposes Committee, it was moved by Mr. Agnew, and seconded by Mr. Barton, "That the road near Moncaster Arms, which is in a very bad state, be repaired; and a weighing machine having been put down there the committee are of opinion that it is too high for the road, and think they are not justified in raising the road at the ratepayers' expense. If Mr. Pennington will meet the Board with regard to the expense they recommend the work to be done in accordance."—The minutes were confirmed.— A telegram was received from Mr. Pennington stating that he had missed the train, and was consequently ur.able ts be present.

FINANCE. At a meeting of the Finance Committee,accountaamornt- ing to £ll4 13s. were examined and ordered to be paid. There was collected and paid into bank since last meeting £l3l 4s. 7d., leaving a balance in bank of £l6 lie. 7d.—The minutes were

HEALTH OF THE DISTHICT. The MEDICAL OFFICER reported as follows:—The health of the district continues fairly satisfactory. I have to report the occurrence of diphtheria at Coach-road, such being the cause of two deaths. Means are being used respecting tho water supply; bat I would certainly advise you still ftrther to impress upon the minds of the persons who ought to supply their tenants with an efficient supply of water during the present excessively hot weather, the thorough urgency of such being at cone done, as we are unaware of what pro- bably may occur. lam unaware of anything further to report. Deaths three, two- being the result of diphtheria. the other unimportant. Births 16."—A fetter was read front the proprietors of Fraser's disinfectant apparatus, asking the Itomd to join with others in the district in the purchase of ' apparatus for disinfecting purposes, the cost of which wolld be J. BTRCHALL was of opinion that they could easily hire one when they wanted one.—The CHAIRMAN' I think that will be the better way.—This was agreed to.

WESLEYAN MEM 'DIST CONFERENCE IN I IYERP OL. On Tuesday, the 138th Conference of "the people called Methodists "commenced in the Brunswick Chapel, Liver- pool. At a little after eight o'clock the doors of the chapel ' were opened, and for an hour and a half members of the Conference slowly gathered. The Conference will be re- vnarkable as one of the largest ever known. During the period of waiting for the opening services on Tuesday, one topic of conversation which caused great sadness was the death of Dean Stanley; who was a consistent friend to Wesleyan Methodism, and who was revered and beloved not less by Methodists than by members of his own communion. The Rev. E. E. Jenkins, M.A., the president of the past ' year, presided.—ln consequence of the absence of the Rev. 'CM. C. Osborn (late secretary of the Conference) the President requested the Rev. R. N. Young, the senior assistant secretary, to take the preliminary duties of the Conference. The roll of the Legal Conference—or the Legal Hundred, as it is popularly called—was then read, when it appeared that during the year four of the number had died—viz., Revs. Dr. Jobson, Dr. Punshon, S. Coley, and W. 0. Simpson. In addition to these, twenty-seven members of the hundred were absent through age, infirmity, &c.—The Secretary moved that a dispensation be granted to the members of the legal hundred who were absent.—This was granted.—The Conference next proceeded to fill up the vacancies in the legal hundred which had been caused by death. The vacancies through death being four, two places were filled by seniority by an election by members of the legal hundred alone—the result being that the Revs. Charles Carter and J. S. Jones received the honour. On the vote being taken for the other two vacancies, the Rev. F. W. Briggs was elected by 154 votes, the next highest being the Rev. D. J. Waller, who received 92 votes. This vote having ' been confirmed by the hundred, Mr. Briggs, who succeeds the late Dr. Punshon, acknowledged his election in fitting terms.

div.p: ST. HELENS POLICE COURT.

MONDAY—Before Messrs. H. A. Bright and T. Pilkington. DAMAGING THE LOCKUPS.—Patrick Kelly was charged with being drunk in Liverpool-road on Saturday. He was also charged with damaging the cleset of the police cell.— P.C. Sherriff proved the charge of drunkenness, and Sergt. Gillighan deposed to hearing prisoner break the lid of the closet and the hinges of the trap door at 8-30 p.m. on Saturday.—Prisoner was ordered to pay 3s 61, the amount of damage, and lOs and costs, or in default 14 days' im- prisonment. DAMAGING e. WINDOW—Maria Lowrie, a married woman, pleaded guilty to committing a breach of the peace by fighting in Sutton-street, Sutton, on the 16th July, and to breaking a pane of glass in a window of the house occupied by Catherine Feeney.—She was bound over to keep the peace for six months on the first charge, and on the latter was fined 58 and costs (4s) and the amount of damage (58), or seven days. AN INCORRIGIBLE DRUNKARD—Luke Connolly, of Parr, made his 42nd appearance in the court for being drunk and disorderly.—The Bench said defendant was perfectly incor- rigible, and he would have to go to prison for one month •with hard labour. ASSISTING THE FIRE Betnenn.—An elderly man named James Travis was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Monday night in Church-street—P.C. Parker said a fire was raging in a yard occupied by Messrs. Webster and Son. Defendant was drunk, and was rushing up the yard and making a great disturbance. He said he was a fireman, and gave witness the name of James Brannon.—Defendant (sharply): I what? Will you tell lies? I gave my own name.—Witness (proceeding) said he afterwards made enquiries, and ascertained that defendant Bad been in the brigade, but it was some years ago. Defendant was a very great nuisance on the night in question.—Defendant said he WAS going up street at 20 minutes to 11, when he heard a woman shrieking behind the door of the yard, and saying that there was a fire in the loft: He had promised to assist the brigade, and was endeavouring to do so when a police- man got hold of him violently, "and it was five minutes before begot a bit of breath."—Mr. Bright: Travis, I am very sorry to see you here. You will have to pay 5s and costs—Defendant: how can I pay it when I have no money to pay it with, eh? (Laughter.) A CAUTION TO PUBLICANS.—John Fife, landlord of the Rising.: Sun publicehouse' East-street, was charged with keeping his premises open for the sale of liquor during pro- hibited honre, and also with unlawfully permitting drun- kenness —P C Parker said that at five minutes past eleven on Wednesday night he passed the defendant's house, and went up the entry to have a look round. A woman came outside, and the door was bolted after her. Some minutes ifterwards he heard voices inside. He listened, and satisfied himself that something wrong was going on in the house. He then went out of the entry and informed P.C.'s Addison and Kendall of what he had heard and seen, and they stationed themselves, P. C's Addison and Kendall in one entry and witness in the other. At 20 minutes past eleven the door was unbolted by the defendant, and a woman came out. He asked the de- fendant what he was doing to have his house open at that time of the night, aud he replied that someone was knocking and he had come to open the door. Witness then asked the woman if she had had neything to drink inside, and she said she had had two glasses of porter. Witness saw some drink of a dark colour in a glass on the counter. It was 21 minutes past eleven by the clock in the bar, and 23 minutes past byjwitnese's own watch. P. C's Addison and Kendall gave corroborative evidence.—Mr. Swift, who appeared for the defendant, submitted there was no case. Defendant was entitled to the benefit of the doubt, and he was quite eine after the long conference their worships had had with the clerk, that there was some doubt about it. The Act of Parliament created different offences, and there was not a tittle of evidence that any drunkenness was permitted ta take place there, and that being so, he was sure their wor- shine would never stretch the evidence to make a convic- tion. About the other case there was not a shadow of a case. A person could not be summoned for one offence and convicted for the other. The house was most respectably conducted, and Messrs. Walker and Co., Wrexham, who owned the house' always pat in respectable managers; and during the 16 or 20 years they had had the house, there had never been a word against it.—Mr. Bright said as regarded the keeping open the licensed premises, they entirely agreed with Mr. Swift that the case had fallen through, for the house being barred, and the bolt being withdenwn, there was no evidence that it was left open. As regarded the other case, there was evidence that the woman came out of the house in a drunken condition. The wording al the Act was a little vague, and it was difficult to know whether it meant that the landlord WS9 liable when a persoa was sup-, plied with drink in a drunken state, or when the drunken- ness took place in the home. There was no douot that she did come out in a drunken state—unless some evidence was adduced strong enough to upset that—and that ahe had two glasses of porter in the house. Those two glasses of beer might have been the finishing stroke to the drunkenness of the woman.—Mr. Swift said that the Act contemplated that a drunken person may be in the house without drunkenness having been permitted to take place there; and further, it contemplated that intoxicating liquors may be sold to a drunken person, which was unlawful, and punishable. It was under that the defendant ought to have been sum- moned—Fife was then put into the box and be denied that the woman was in the house at all. The woman W2ft knock- ing at the door, and when he went to order the woman away, the officer shoved "her in.—Mr. Bright: Do you say that she was net in the bowie at all.—Witness: I don't beFleve she was.—Jas. Foster, butcher, Eccleston-lane, said he left the house of defendant at five minutes to eleven, and defendant wee then preparing to olose.—Mr. Johnson: Well, our case does ' not begin until five ninnies afler. —Mr. Bright: I must sayl that your witnesses do not command our confidence. At one or two points they contradict one another. and contradict , the officers totally—unless the officers were committing per- j jury which we do not believe. He will be fined £5 and costs ' or one month's imprisonment. —Mr. Swift: Your worships won't fine him £5 for the first offence. In Liverpool they j don't fine above 105. unless it is a bad case.—Mr. Bright: From the evidence we consider this is a bad case, and we cannot trust the man at all. A SERIOUS FIGHTIN PARR-STaEET.—Peter Lawton, Parr, was charged with assaulting Frank Riley, on Monday last.' —lt appeared from the evidence that on Monday night a j disturbance arose behind complainant's house in Parraetreet. Defendant was assaulting complainant's father-in-law, and the friends and relatives of each party assembled, and a general fight commenced. Pdkers, bricks, basins, and other weapons and missiles were need, and it was alleged that defendant struck complainant on the head with a hammer, and knocked him senseless. He WU taken to a doctor and his head was dressed.—Mr. Riley appeared for the complainant and Mr. Swift for the defendant, and after evidence of a,very conflicting nature had been given the magistrates dismissed the case; saying that it was impossible to decide upon which side the truth ley. There had been a great deal of lying and perjury. Lneynea WORK WITHOUT NOTlM—Thomas Swift,col- lier, wan summoned far not carrying out his contract, and the Crank coil company claimed £2 as damages sustained by defendant leaving work without notice.—Mr. Swift, called Richard Ball, under-looker at the colliery who proved the case, and the defendant who did not appear was fined J £1 as damages, and the costa, - AN OLD OFFENDER "SETTLES. THEM OFF."—Johßi'arr, an elderly man, was charged under the Game Act, on ens- picion, with coming from land with game in his poceession. Mr. Swift appe ired on the part of Colonel Gamble who pre- serves the game in the locality where the detection took place. The information was laid under the act of Parlia- ment passed to prevent poaching, and which authorised police constables to stop suspected persons on the highway, and search them; and if game he found upon them to seize the game, and afterwards summon them. On Sunday morn- ing P. C. Ratcliffe met defendant with a greyhound, nearly full-bred, and after bidding him "good morning "asked him what he had got ander his shirt. He examined defendant and found a rabbit skilfully hidden under his shirt, and put round his body, as far as possible, to conceal it. The rabbit was quite warm and bleeding, and was carrying seven young ones. On being asked where he got the rabbit defendant re- plied that " God " had given it to him.—lnspector Wood read a list of defendant's previous convictions from which it appeared defendant had been convicted under the Game Laws in 1843, 1856, 1362, and 1874.—Defendant : Mr. Swift bast told you that a rabbit is game, and it is not game, it is "varmint." (Laughter.)—Mr. Bright : You are an old poacher, and you will be fined 20s. and costs or 14 d Defendant : li. had sooner go 14 days than pay a penny. I Would so; that's the way to settle them off. He WAS then t ikan downstairs. _

Alfred Moore, labourer, who on the night of Friday last strangled his wife at Stafford, was on Thursday convicted° murder and sentenced to death. A main line train ran into a North Kent train which was standing at London Bridge Statison yesterday afternoon, injuring a large number of passengers, those most severely hurt being removed to Guy's Hospital. The accident is believed to have occurred through defective points.

div.head: ELECTION OF PRESIDENT AND SECRETARY.
div.p: ELECTION OF PRESIDENT AND SECRETARY.

The Conference then elected by ballot Dr. Osborn as president, and Rev. R. N. Young as secretary. The legal hundred by a special vote duly confirmed these elections.— Mr. Jenkins then vacated the presidential chair, and Dr. Osborn stepping forward occupied it, while the whole Con- ference rose to its feet heartily shaking hands with the newly-elected president. The ex-president handed over to the president Mr. Wesley's Bible and the Conference Seal, and congratulated him on his election by so large a vote.— Dr. Osborn, in reply, said his first atknowledgments were due to his heavenly Father' by whose goodness he found himself in circumstances which warranted his acceptance of that wholly unsought and, until lately, unexpected honour. They knew him well enough to know how highly he prized that vote. They and their fathers had known him all their lives. There were very few around him in that Conference whose entry into the ministry he was not cognisant of, and in whose career he had not taken personal interest. To his utmost astonishment he found himself the oldest man who had sat in that chair with the exception of Mr. Wesley him- self. He had seen in it Mr. Atherton, Mr. Reece twice, Mr. H. Moore twice, Dr. Newton four times, Dr. Bunting four times, Dr. Clarke three times, and others none of whom at the period of his last election had reached the age which he (Dr. Osborn) reached a few weeks ago. If he mentioned that he did it in gratitude to God, who had helped him all his life, and who would not leave him then. He remembered when going in 1824 as a youth to preach his trial sermon as a local preacher, his heart beat hard, and the last thing he did before leaving his bedroom was to open his Bible, when his eye fell upon the passage, "What time I am afraid I will trust in Thee." How often had he blessed God for that word. He felt fear that day, not of them, but of himself , but he cast himself on the old promise which a thousand times he had found true. The ex-President had said his eyes were not dim and his natural strength was not abated, He fancied that was a case in which the wish was father to the thought. In looking into the coming Conference he knew they would be indulged, and God would be faithful, and what mere could they desire to secure a happy and use- ful Conference? What he was afraid of was lest anything should come to, mar the glorious work of God, which after years of declinal had been followed by a year of progress 4 He trusted that such a gracious influence might come upon them that they would all go forth baptised afresh for their work.—The Rev. R. N. Young, in acknowledging his election to the position of -secretary, said the Methodist Conference was always gewrous and always gracious, and he regarded the honour he had just received as a tribute to the honoured name he bore, and as a recognition of the fact that for thirteen years he had done his best in the work of that platform.

div.head: NEW PRESIDENT.
div.p: THE NEW PRESIDENT.

The Rev. George-5:1);;;D-.57,--th-Ernewly-elested Presi- dent of the Wesleyan Conference' is a native of Rochester, where his family long held an honourable position. The date of his birth is 1308, so that he is now in his seventy- third year. His early education, which was of a liberal des- cription, was conducted by Dr. Hulett. In 1829 he entered the Wesleyan ministry, and commenced the itinerancy by two years in the Brighton circuit. In 1831 he removed to ' Liverpool (Pitt-street), where he stayed but one year, at the j close of which he entered the Deptfold circuit, and again stayed but one year. Atter this he travelled the full, term of three years in each of the following, circuits :—Steckport, London (Great Queen.street), London, (City-road) Man- chester (Grosvenor-street), Liverpool (Brunswick), and , Manchester (Oxford-road). Afterwards, for seventeen years, Dr. Osborn was one of the secretaries at the Mission House in London • while in 1868, he wan elected theoiogical tutor at Richmond Missionary College, Surrey. In 1863, Dr. Osborn was previously elected president, and in con- sequence of the deplored death of his successor (Rev. W. L. Thornton). be had nearly two years presidential respon- , sibility. Dr. Osborn has given one of the Fernley leatures, the subject being "The Holy Spirit." The new President , is aline expository preacher, a skilful debater, and a. most able administrator. The vote of Tuesday may be inter- preted as an index of his influence in Methodism.

The Conference continued its sittings at. Brunswick Chapel. The elections for the Legal Hundred completed its formal constitution. Thanks were then voted to thu officers for their services in the past year. The Revs. D. J. Waller, S. Lees, and E. Clapham were elected assistant secretaries. Memorials and suggestions were received, and a committee appointed to consid4er them—The Rev. Anthony Ward (chairman of the Leeds district), brought before toe- Con- ference the hearty and unanimous invitation of the Leeds district that the Conference-of 1882 hhonld assemble in that town. The invitatiomwas for 400 ministers in addition to those in, the fAsecla, district. ~ The Conference agreed to accept the invitation.—The Rev. G. Stringer Rowe is pre- paring the annual address of the Conference to the Media- -1 dist societies. Tha•Revs. Dr. Pope, E. J. Robinson, John I Barker,. and J. S. Banks were appointed a committee to I revise it..

On Monday the members of the Lord Stanley Lodge o the Independent Order of Oddfellows„Manchester. Unity, Prescot district, had their annual dinner at the Stanley Arms Hotel, Roby. Oa Sunday afternoon a number of mem- bers attended divine service at Roby Parish Church, when the vicar, the Rev. G. J. Banner, preached a very appropriate sermon from Romans. xii, verse 5. The anniversary,this year was not on so large a scale as onprevious years, owing, it was said, to the majority of the members attending to take part in the procession at Southport, on the occasion of the meeting of the A.M.O There was no processioa through the district, neither wa. there a brass band, and the custom of allowing the members' wives and friexls into the room after I dinner was also unobserved. Only about 17 or 18 sat down I to dinner, which was of a sumptuous character amongst those present being the Rev. G. J. Banner, P.P.G.M. ;, Richard, Gore, P.P.G.M.; Samuel Green, P.Pki.M. ; Wm. Brennand, P.P.G.M.; Thomas Brown, Prov. DIG.M.; James Bixter, PG.; Henry Rinamer, puti Secretary Huhne. From the balance sheet ended 25th Decem- ber last it appeared that the lodge was in a very prosperous state. In the sick and funeral fund the receipts had been £1.74 4s. Bd., which, together with a balance of £865 15s. 611. brought forward from the previous year, made a total of £1,0400a. 2d. Theexpenditure had been £93 4s. id (including £6l 16s. paid sick members, £3O Bs. to the district funeral fund, 4.), leaving a balance in favour of the fund of £946 16s. lid., an increase of £Bl Os. 74. on the previous year. There had been no expendi- ture in connection with the widow and orphans' fund, the balance in favour of the fund being 13s. Bad. The manage- ment fund accounts showed that the receipts had been £54. 3s. 4d.; balance from previous year, £46 15s. 5d.; total, £lOO 1114. 94.; expenditure, £4O Us. 1d; leaving a balance of £6O Is. 3d., an increase in this fund. of £l3 120., 31. In. the anniversary fund the total receipts made up a sum £24 9a., and the expenses amounted to /23 17a. ld., leaving a balanee of £lls. 11d. The amount of funds at the end of the year was £l,OOB- Os. OeL amount of funds at end of, previous year (1M), £912 108. lltf,k; gain during the year, £95 90 Id. The number of members in January, 1880,'was. 139.: entered during the year, 20i, total, 159. Deduct ten (nine excluded and one died), leaving the number at end of year at 149. The 'average age per member was 30 years, and the average worth £6 14s, 114. After full justice had been done to the good things provided, the chair was taken by P.P..G.M.S. Green, and the vice-chair by Ploy. D.G.M.James The Chairman reed letters of apology for non-attendance from the Rev. Canon Fenrhyn, vicar of Iluyton' and C.S. Benjamin Lawton.—P.P.G...l4. Gore apologised for the absence of his son, Mr. Aaron Gore, the Grand Master of the District.—The following toast list was gone tareugh "The Queen," "Prince and Princess of Wales and rest of Royal Family," "The Army, Navy, and Volunteers," "The Bishop and Clergy of the Diocese and Ministers of all Denominations," "Manchester Unity," "The A.M.C.," " Prosperity to the Prescot District," "The District Officers," "S Prosperity to the Lord Stanley Lodge,, "Theugn, Officers," " s',"Host and Hostess," &e.—At the conclusion of the meeting dancing commenced, and was kept up to a late hour. The approach of Ayoub Khan towards Candahar is re- ported by the Viceroy. It ems reported that the Prinoe had reached Farrah, and a decisive conflict with the Arneers s 1, forces cannot be long delayed. Ayoub appears to have with o strong force, and in his train are several 01-knowit Oirdars.

PRESCOT POLICE COURT. Tuzsztem.--Before Messrs. T. Pilkington and W. L. Evans. RIDING ON TES RAILWAY WITHOOT A TICHET.—Mary Hanley, peosoot, was charged with riding on the London and North-Western Railway, between Lime-street, Liver- pool, and Prescot, without having previously paid her fare; also tr , ted baring wilfully damaged a window. Mr. Preston, ..—Defendant was a traveller in a third-class with corn. partaient of the 11-15 p.m. train from Liverpool. When defendant came to the gate the porter asked for her ticket, and she said she bad not come by the train. There was anothe4 woman with the defendant, and the porter asked her for her ticket. The woman searched for her ticket in her pockets, but as she could not find it she paid her fare applied to, refused to pay. Shortly afterwards the rather than, as she said, "have any bother." Defendant, on being r heard a row in the waiting-room, and on going to see the cause of it he saw defendant holding the other woman by the hair of the head. After remonstrating with them he anrtdbaa ctki to otwh es mboaoskhiendg ionffitheeewanaidtiinmgm-roedo ima e butly a cf ot eur lwd a nr dos het we say whethor the defendant or the other woman broke it.— Benjamin Smith,another porter, said that on the night in question he saw defendant on the station at Lime-street. Witness came by. the 11-15 train to Prescot. Defendant travelled in the same train, and also got out at Prescot. Defendant and another woman had a dispute about some money, and in the quarrel the defendant broke the waiting- room window. Defendant was the worse for liquor. The damage to the window was estimated at 58.—For travelling without a ticket defendant was fined lOs and costs. The

other charge was dismissed. A DANGEROUS PnecTim—William Birch, a young man, was charged with leaving the carriage of a train whilst in motion at Huvton station on the 4th inst.—Mr. Preston, junior, prosecuted on behalf of the railway company', and stated that the defendant was a traveller by the 1-23 p.m. express train from Warrington to Liverpool on the 4th July, and when passing Huyton station defendant jumped out.— William Brown, guard of the train, said that on nearing Huytou station he saw a man jump from the train, but could not say whether defendant was the man or not, as his head was turned to him at the time. As he was passing the Aeon he made motions to the officials to stop the man. —Defendant, who pleaded guilty, was fined the full penalty of 40s. and costs, the Chairman remarking that he had by , his conduct worthily deserved it. WHOLESALE PILFERINGS BY A COOK.—Mary Spencer, a respectably attired young woman, was brought up on remard charged with steling an Indian shawl, table cloth, three bedroom towels, toilet cover, three pieces of cotton, three glass towels, three kitchen towels, dm., value £3 103., the property of Mr. George Gerald Smart, of Sandown- lane, Wavertree.—lnspector Barnett stated that the case had been brought up at Wootton and the deposition taken, but it ould not be dealt with owing to there being only one magi- strate present.—Prosecutor's wife stated that prisoner was in her husband's employ as cook from the 21st April to the Bth Jnly. Witness left home in May, leaving the prisoner in charge of the house. She came back again on the 25th June, and shortly afterwards missed some knives from the cbeffonier drawers in the dining-room. Witness asked the prisoner what had become of them, and she said she did not know. She had never seen them, and could swear no one had been in the house during witness's absence. On making an examination witness missed a large number of articles, and information was given to the police. The articles pro- duced were her husband's property.—Other evidence was, given as to.the finding of the articles produced in the pri- soner's possession.—Prisoner pleaded guilty.—The Chair- man said she had not only stolen the articles, but she had been guilty o a breach of trust, and she would have to go to prison or six months. THEFT OF A WATCH: A QUEER HIDING PLACE—John Jackson was charged with stealing a silver watch, value £3, the property of a young woman named Ann Ralphs. Pro- , secntrix had lodged for about two months at a house in] Rathbone-road, Weavertree, where the prisoner had also been in the habit of lodging. On Monday, the 11th instant,' prisoner came to the house to lodge, and late in the evening prosecutrix missed the watch from her bedroom. She ques- tioned the prisoner about it, but be denied having seen R. Prosecrutrix then gave information to the police.—Elizabeth Bettisford, Rathbone-road, said the prisoner asked her to I lend him some money on a watch. Witness refused, sayingi she did not "keep a pawnshop." The watch produced semi the same the prisoner offerred to her.—P.C. Porter deposed to apprehending the prisoner, who, in an, ,-,•r to a question he put to him, said the watch was hid , a the bed-room chimney. Witness searched the chimney and found the watch.—Prosecutrix identified the watch as her property., —Prisoner said he had been taking drink • irher freely of I late, and did not know what he was doing when he took the watch.—Sentenced to one month's imprisonment with hard labour. Romartm A PIGEON COTE.—John Gillard and Edward Fitzsimmons, two boys, were charged with having stolen 26 pigeons, the property of Henry Lyon, Paradise Gardens, Weavertree.—About ten o'clock en Thursday night, the 3th ult., prosecutor locked up his pigeon-cote, containing 40 pigeons. On the following morning he found the cote had been broken open and 26 birds taken away. The birds which stolen were worth about 328. The same morning one the boys offered some pigeons for sale .. a poultry dealer's, but the dealer's suspicions being aroused he told the boy he thought be had stolen them. The boy then ran out of the shop followed by the dealer, who eventually caught him and headed him over to a policeman. The other boy was seen going along Oldham-street by another constable, who, I noticing that the boy looked rather bulky about the body, followed him. The boy ran up an entry, where he was secured, and seven pigeons fund under his coat.—Prisoners were each committed to gaol for one month. COAL STEALING AT Wurerow.—Mary Braney, a middle- aged woman, was charged with stealing coal from the Cans Colliery, Whiston.—Joseph Storey, foreman at the colliery, said that on the 30th June he saw defendant pick up and carry away about Icwt. of coal.—A line of 20s. and costs was inflicted. Oarthenni RELIEF BY FALSE PRETENCES.—On the ap- plication of Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Guardians; a warrant was granted for the apprehension of a man named , James Taylor, who bad obtained relief under false pretences at St. Helens. RF.AVY FINES FOR ASSAULT AT RAINHILL.—Sarah Critchley was summoned for assaulting John Lewis Priee and hie wife, Mary Pricer and Robert Critchley, her son, was summoned for assaulting John Price.—Mr. Swift ap- peared for the complainants, and Mr. Tvrer tor the defen- dants.—Mr. Swift said the assaults weee committed on the 12th July. Complainants were sitting down at dinner when defendants went to the back door of the house occupied by Price and his family, and shouted' for the father and son to come out, the two lads saying they would fight either father or son. Mrs. Price went to the door and tried to persuade the defendants to go away, when Mrs. Critchley ran at her seized her by the hair of the head, struck her on the head, face, and breast, and then knocked her into the hedge. Whilst she was in the hedge the female defendant assaulted her in a most brutal manner. Mrs. Price then ran away for a policeman. In the meantime Robert Critchley and Ids brother Thomas ran into the house aad assaulted John Lewis Price by knocking him down and beating him while he was on the ground, and the female defendant also struck him several times. When Mrs. Price returned with a policeman, she found the house in a disorderly state and her husband covered with blood.—Evidence in support of this statement was given by the complainant and several witnesses—For the defence it was contended that the defendants went to the complainant's house,. and that Price threatened tostrike the female defendant with a poker which he carried is his hand. To prevent this Mrs. Price's two Sons put the male complainant on the ground.—Witnesses were called in sup- port of this version of the affair, but in answer to Mr. Swift they admitted that Mrs. Critchley had hit Mrs. Price.—The Bench characterized the case as a very bed one, and fined Mrs. Critchloy 50a. and costs for the assault on each of the complainants, and Robert Critchlev was also fined 50s. for the assault on John Lewis Price.—On the application of Mr. I Swift, the Bench allowed 10s.' out of each of the fines Lopes, towards the advocate's fee.

The Very Rev. A. P. Stanley, D.D., the Dean of West. minster, died on Monday evening, in the 66th year of his _
age. By his death the Church of England lose; one of the
most eloquent of her divines, and literature one of its
brightest ornaments. His voice was invariably raised on

the side of freedom and tolerance, and the nation is the I poorer for the death of one whose fame was world-wide as a I ripe scholar, a great pulpit orator, and a brilliant writer. The Dean was somewhat seriously indisposed last week, but the worst was not apprehended until Sunday. The preacher at Westminster Abbey on Sunday evening was the Bishop of Manchester, the Dean's valued and affectionate friend; and the mo.t painful impression was made upon a vast con- gregation by the Bishop's solemn and affecting reference to Dean Stanley's condition. The Dean will be buried beside the remains of Lady Augusta Stanley, his wife, in West- minster Abbey. It is thought that the original cause of the erysipelas, to which the deceased succumbed, was blood poisoning, consequent on his having inhaled some noxious vapours—where, cannot at present be stated with accuracy. Arthur Penrhyn StanleY was born on the 13th December„ 1815, at Alderley' of which place his father, afterwards Bishop of Norwich, was the incumbent. The elder Stanley was widely known for his literary and scientific attainments before Lord Melbourne gave him his bishopric in 1837. During his 32 years at Alderley he had published a "History of Birds," and became a fellow of the Royal Society and of the Linnseara Society. His theological views were known to be liberal, they were spoken of as latitudinarian, and his addresses and charges, his sermons and pamphlets, were often the occasion of much controversy; and foreshadowed some views which have since been more widely accepted in the Church. His son was sent to Rugby, of which Dr. Arnold was then head-master; and the younger Stanley be- came deeply imbued with an influence to which some of the ; best elements of English life in the present day owe much of their force if not even their origin. From Rugby he went to %Rio), where he had gained a scholarship. He was I afterwards elected a Fellow of University College, and for I 12 years was Tutor of his College. It was in this period ' of his life that the chief works by which he will be remem-

bared were writteu. He became Regius Professor of Eccle- siastical History in 1858, and it was in this professorate that his Lectures on the History of the Eastern Church and his Lectures on the Jewish Church were delivered and pub-, lished. In these works his great faculty for a picturesque reproduction of the men and scenes of the past was strikingly shown. The rongh men who gathered to the Council of Nimes, the quarrels and struggles of the Council itself in the elaboration of the Nicene Creed, live and move before us on his pages.. His interest in the Eastern Church was mani-

• fested durino, his journey to the East, in company with the Prince of Wales, an lccount of which he published in an appendix to" Sermons preached in the East." In 1863 he was appointed by Lord Palmerston to the Deanery of West- minster, an office which he has made popular and powerful for 18 years. Those years have not been without con- troversy. There was a strong opposition to his appointment in 1872 as one of the select preachers at Oxford, but on a poll he was elected by 349 votes against 287. In 1875 he was elected Rector of the University of St. Andrews. His life of his father, the late Bishop of Norwich, and the "Life and Correspondence of Dr. Arnold," his teacher were amongst his earliest works, and as admirable biographies, as well as warm testimonies of personal affection, gained for him at once a position in literature. His other works are so numerous that they could merely be catalogued here. Few public events of late years have happened without a sermon by Dean Stanley taking up their religious meaning, and pointing an instructive moral from them. It is somewhat singular that the loving guardian of the treasures of West- minster Abbey had little love of art, to which, in fact, he was comparatively indifferent, or of music for which be had no sense. But he approached the Abbey from its historic side; and as the great home of England's dead he saw in it that to which his historic faculty could cling. He has left it better known and more honoured than it ever was before it came into his generous keeping. The Daily News states that the Dean's illness was brought lon by a chill which he caught on Thursday, July 7, at the annual flower show of the Society for Promoting Window Gardening among the working- classes in the parishes of St. Margaret and St. John, Westminster, which was held in the College gardens, under the presidency of Lord Shaftesbury. He felt unwell on the following day; and on Saturday, after preaching a short sermon in the Abbey, he complained of sickness. His health passed through various vicissi- tudes in the following week, but it appears that on Wednes- day last he was well enough to receive company. Subse- quently erysipelas set in, and his constitution gradually succumbed to the attack. Convocation for the Southern Province, in the proceedings of which Dean Stanley always took a prominent part, met on Tuesday for business: The Primate said Dean Stanley's death was a great loss to the National Church. The aim of his life had been to make Westminster Abbey a national institution, as was evidenced from his last audible words, which were "I have laboured amidst many frailties and much weakness to use this insti- tution, the great centre of religious and national life, in a truly liberal spirit." Convocation adjourned for a short space-in respect to the Dean's memory.

div.head: CE'.NSUS OF LANCASHIRY.
div.p: THE CE'.NSUS OF LANCASHIRY.

The population of Lancashire is said to be 3454,225, an increase of 634,730 in ten years. Of this total 1,667,370 were males, and 1.784246 females. There were 655.493 in- hal.ited houses, 67,425 were uninhabited, and 5,768 were being built. Excluding the boroughs, there were 273,417 inhabitants in the Northern Division, 238,544 in the North- Fastern Ditision, 534.963 in the South-Eastern Division,. and 482,148 in the South-Western Parliamentary Division. div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

CHRIST CHURCH, WINSFORD.—Sermons on behalf of the Weaver Church Sunday School were preached on Sunday last by the Rey. J. W. Hill, M.A., rector of Waverton, Chester. The school was used in place of the church, which is not yet erected, but it was well filled, and the col- lections were quite equal to former years. In the afternoon the Rev. E. Nixon, M.A., incumbent of the church, gave an address to the scholars and parents, &c. OVER.—The anniversary services in connection with the Over Congregational Sunday School were held on Sunday last, when two sermons were preached by the Rev. W. A. Gutteridge, M.A., of Cambridga, to overflowing an appre- ciative audiences. The sermon in the morning was on "Samuel's call," and that in the evening on the " Lord's Prayer ;" both gave great satisfaction. The collections amounted to £2l 7s. sd. CAMP MEETING, SWANLOW-LAHE.—The United Metho- dist Free Church of Winston/ and Weaver, and the Wesleyans, had a camp meeting, on Sunday last, in a field behind the Wesleyan Chapel, when addresses were given by the Rev. E. Sheers, 8A.., and Messrs. J. Hulse and Griffihs, Burrows, Joseph Buckley (Gate House, Middlewich), &c. The attendance was very good both afternoon and evening. CLUB FRSTITAL.—The members of the Ancient Order of Forresters had their annual walk on Saturday followed by a dinner at the White Lion, Over. The Rifle Volunteer band accompanied the procession, and added to the enjoy- ment by their lively strains. A WOMAN BURNED AT WINSFORD.—A lamentable case' of burning occurred at Winsford, on Saturday. A young woman named Carden, who lives with Mrs. Carden, at the tea rooms, Gravel Hill, was near the fire when her dress caught, and before the flames could be extinguished, she was so badly burnt that her recovery is doubtful. DROWNING CASE AT DARNHALL.—A little boy named William Thomas Baker, whose father is a labourer at Darn- hall, accidentally fell into a pit during the temporary ab- sence of his mother at the milk factory, and was drowned. An inquest was held, on Monday, before Mr. Churton, and a verdict of accidental death returned by the jury, who re- I commended that the mother should get someone to look alter .. her children during her absence.

The balance of profits will then be div.ded as follows ;-50 per cent. thereof to the Preference Shares, and the balance to the Ordi- nary Shares. THE MID-CHESHIRE SALT AND CHEMICAL COMPANY, LIMITED. InOorporated under the Companies' Act, 1862 to 1880, whereby the liability of members is limited to the amount of their Shares. CAPITAL £250,000 in £50,000 Shares of £5 each. This Company is formed for the purpose of erecting works, and carrying on the business of Salt and Chemical Manufac- turers, on a very extensive scale, at Middlewich, in the County of Chester. and generally for the pnrporaf specified in the filemotandum of Association. Great Salt deposits.exist at Middlewich and other places in the County of Chester. and brine is raised or pumped from these deposits, and manufactured by evaporation into salt for home and foreige consumption. In addition to over half a million tons used at home over one million tons were exported last year The Cheshire salt district yields by far the greatest portio-; of the supply; in fact, it has practically the monopoly ,f supplying the world with salt, furnishing, as it does, 1 000,000 tons per annum for expert from Liverpool, and up. wards of 400,000 tons to the chemical works of Widnes and other towns. There can be no doubt that the salt trade is one of the most important mineral industries to the kingdom. The trade is also& most profitable one. The manufacture of chemical-, which salt is most exten• 'lively used, is also a very profitabln. !fatness. For the commencement of operato n. an eligible site, con. tabling about five a half acres, on whir.. tluable brine eprings or runs exist, situate at Kinderton, Mid !ewich, in the County of Chester, and adjacent both to canal and railway, has been secured for the first works of the Company on advantageous terms, the purchase money for which (20,000) will be paid by the allotment to the Vendors of 1,00 fully paid.up Ordinary Shares, and the I alance (213,000) in cash. The estate is freehold, and beneath the surface of the soil is a very fine bed of clay, from which all the bricks for the erection of the necessary works and buildings can be made. This will save a considerable outlay in the cost of the works, On one porthin 01 the estate there is a valuable bed of sand, which can be used in the building of the proposed works of the Company. There is also a large mansion and outbuildings, suitable for the residence of a Manager and for the Company's offices on the estate. ' The Company will be prepared to adopt the best machinery, methods, and patents which may be invented from time to time for the manufacture of both sit and chemicals. This Company will raise the brine for salt making from its own land, and will thus save the royalty or rate of 61). per ton of salt ordinarily paid by salt makers in the district for brine. This alone will effect, a great saving in the manufacture of salt of this Company; and, in addition to this, the saving in the price of the cost and carriage of salt to be used in the manufac- ture oh chemicals by this Company (salt having to be purchased by other chemical man ufactures) will be very great The Salt Works at both Northwich and Winsford are subject to occasional stoppages and to great damage and disablement, caused by subsidences of the lad, in consequence of the large and contnnual extraction of salt-rock and brine therefrom. The Works of this Company will be erected upon solid virgin ground, some miles distant from these sinking places. The brine at Middlewich is also of a better class and of greater strength for salt makirg purposes than that got either at Northwich or Winsford, and a new source of supply such as the one now proposed to be worked will be of incalcu- lable value. The site of the proposed Works, being in close proximity to ' to the Trent and Mersey Canal, and abutting on the London I and 7, on th-Western Railway, this Company can lead its manu- factures direct into railway wagons at the Works, and will consequently be able to save a considerable amount paid by other manufacturers at Middlewich for cartage to the rail- way. The subsequent erection or purchase of other works at suit- aNe places in the district is also contemplated. The extiting salt and chemical works in the Cheshire districts ate doing prosperous and increasing trades, and from the known remunerative character of both businesses the Directors are of opinion that the Share Capital of this Compauy will even in times of depre,sion in trade earn a minimum profit of 15 per cent, per annum, and that these dividends in active seasons will be largely increased, and they are satisfied that the shares of this Company will be a sound and lucrative investment. It is estimated that the present issue of capital will be amply sufficient to enable the Directors to complete the pur- chase of the estate named, and to erect and finish works thereon to a large and paying extent, as well as provide a sufficient surplus with which to commence business. !Tlre vendors of the site and brine springs already selected for the first works of the Company are so satisfied with the pros pacts of the undertaking that they have agreed to depo•it ordi- , racy ftv ly paid up shares f the Company to the value of ! £7.000 with he D rectors for two years, as a security for the payment of a dividend of 7ji per cent, per annum on the pre- lerence shares of the company. ! Appllnation will be made in due course to the Stock Ex- change for an official quotation of the shares of the Company.
